item.title: We made it okay to talk. Getting help is still too hard.
item.description: A student on the gap between talking about mental health and finding care: 137 million people in shortage areas, providers with full caseloads, and four small things to try this week.
item.content:encoded:
Note before we begin: this post talks about mental health care and mentions suicide. No methods are described. If you or someone near you is in crisis, call or text 988 (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline) in the US, or call 911 for an emergency.

For about ten years we have been told to talk about our mental health. Schools say it. Brands say it. Everybody says it. So people try. They finally say the words, and then they hit a wall.

I’m a grad student training to be a family therapist, so I can see the other side of that wall too. Good clinicians are full. Waitlists are long. Nobody is being lazy. There just aren’t enough of us yet.

The numbers

Here is what the government’s own data says.

  • About 137 million people in the US, roughly 40 percent of the country, live in an area the federal government labels a Mental Health Professional Shortage Area (HRSA, State of the Behavioral Health Workforce, 2025).
  • In a 2025 report, the HHS Inspector General found that 45 percent of surveyed behavioral health providers were not available to take a new patient on Medicare or Medicaid. Of those, 73 percent said they could not take any new patients at all, and many pointed to full caseloads. Among providers who were available, about one in four had a wait of more than 30 days (HHS OIG, report OEI-09-21-00410).
  • In 2024, Asian American adults were 45 percent less likely than US adults overall to have received mental health treatment in the past year. Suicide was the leading cause of death for Asian Americans ages 15 to 24 in 2022 (HHS Office of Minority Health).

That last one matters to me. I’m Vietnamese American. In my house, feelings usually got brushed off instead of talked about, and I know I’m not the only one who grew up that way. I don’t say that to blame my parents. They were working hard and getting through the day. I say it because silence at home and a shortage of providers stack on top of each other. A person who finally gets brave enough to ask can still find nobody to ask.

A note on the numbers. Asian Americans overall die by suicide at a lower rate than the US average, and Asian American adults were 27 percent less likely to report a mental illness in 2024. The treatment gap is still real, and so is the youth number. Both can be true.

Why it happened

I don’t have one clean answer, and I don’t think anyone does. Reports I have read point to low pay for many counseling jobs, long training, burnout, and rural areas with few or no providers. Many providers also do not take insurance, and many insurance networks list providers who never see a single patient. In the 10 counties the OIG studied, an average of 55 percent of the behavioral health providers listed in Medicare Advantage plans did not provide a single service to enrollees in 2023 (HHS OIG, OEI-02-23-00540).

Add stigma on top, and the people who most need the door are the ones least able to find it.

What the gap costs

When someone gets brave once and fails, they may not try twice. I’m a student and I can’t speak for everyone, so I’ll say only this. Quietly giving up looks like a likely ending to a hard search for help, and it never shows up in a statistic about people who got treated.

A few small things that might help

I think talking was step one, and step two is building the door people walk through. I don’t have the big fix. Here are a few small things I’m trying to practice, and they take about ten minutes this week.

  1. Ask one person. Text someone you care about and ask when they last tried to find help, and what happened. Then listen. Don’t fix.
  2. Ask your local government. Find your state or county mental health agency and ask what is being done about provider shortages where you live. Send your state representative the same question. Short and polite works.
  3. Be the logistics. Drive someone, watch their kids, or make the follow-up call with them. A lot of access comes down to logistics, and logistics can be changed.
  4. Save 988. Put it in your phone and tell one other person you did. You can call or text.

I’m still learning how to do this well, and I want to keep reading the data and listening to how people actually try to find help.

I’m a student sharing what I’m learning. This isn’t therapy or clinical advice.

Sources

  • HRSA, State of the Behavioral Health Workforce, 2025
  • HHS OIG, Availability of Surveyed Behavioral Health Providers to Treat New Patients Enrolled in Medicare and Medicaid (OEI-09-21-00410), June 2025
  • HHS OIG, Many Medicare Advantage and Medicaid Managed Care Plans Had Limited Behavioral Health Networks (OEI-02-23-00540)
  • HHS Office of Minority Health, Mental and Behavioral Health, Asian Americans

item.title: The queue is the policy: who pays the hidden time tax?
item.description: A student's argument that waiting quietly decides who can use a system: Social Security phone wait times, who can afford to hold, my own disability insurance paperwork, and one redesign.
item.content:encoded:
Start with the phone call

Pick one everyday system: calling the government for benefits. I’m using Social Security’s national 800 number because it publishes its wait times, which most systems don’t.

Here is what the Social Security Administration’s own inspector general reported for fiscal year 2025 (October 2024 to September 2025). Callers who stayed on hold waited on average about 51 minutes in October 2024, and about 1 hour 40 minutes at the worst point in January 2025. By September 2025 that had dropped to 19 minutes. Callers who took a callback waited an average of about 109 minutes for it, and the callback wait peaked at 2 hours 32 minutes. Callers who gave up and hung up had waited between about 22 and 38 minutes on average, depending on the month.

That is a real improvement by the end of the year, and the agency says so. It is also worth knowing how the headline number works. The agency’s “average speed of answer” counts anyone who accepts a callback as a zero-minute wait, and it leaves out the time they wait for the call back. So the number people see is smaller than the time people spend.

Who can afford that wait

A wait is cheap if you have a desk job, a private phone and a boss who doesn’t mind. It gets expensive in other places.

If you’re paid by the hour, a 50-minute hold is 50 minutes you aren’t earning, or a call you take on break and hope doesn’t drop. Paid sick leave is a rough stand-in for whether you can step away: in March 2026, 83 percent of all civilian workers had access to it, but only 63 percent of workers in the lowest-paid quarter and 48 percent in the lowest-paid tenth did.

If you have a disability, a long hold can mean sitting, pressing buttons, or talking when that is the hard part. If you’re caring for someone, you may not get a long stretch where nobody needs you.

Annie Lowrey calls this the “time tax” in her book of that name: the hours lost to paperwork, phone calls and lines to get things people qualify for. She says the people charged the most are often the ones with the least time and money. She points to Wisconsin in spring 2020, where she says the state didn’t answer 99.5 percent of unemployment calls. Those are her words in an NPR interview, so I’m treating that number as her claim and not an audited figure.

The turn: waiting decides who gets in

My argument is that time isn’t only wasted in a queue. The way a system makes people wait quietly decides who is able to use it.

Nobody writes “people with hourly jobs may not apply.” But if the only way in is a long hold during business hours, the people who can’t take that hold are screened out, and nobody ever has to say so. The queue works like an eligibility rule that isn’t written down. That is my reading of the evidence above, and you can disagree with it.

My own experience

The numbers above come from Social Security because it publishes them. My own experience was applying for disability insurance, and I think the same pattern shows up there. The part that wore me down was the paperwork and getting my doctors to fill out their forms. I lost count of how many hoops there were.

The best way I can describe it is a check engine light that keeps coming back on. You deal with it, and then it pops up again. It’s one more form, one more thing to chase, one more thing sitting in the back of your mind. For a while I wondered if I was just being lazy.

Looking back, I don’t think that’s the right question. The system asked me to keep track of a lot of small tasks, and each one depended on someone else getting back to me.

One idea I’d like to see tried

I’m not a policy expert, but one idea seems worth trying: a callback that works for the caller. The Social Security Administration already offers callbacks, but callers don’t get an estimated wait for them, and the average was about 109 minutes. I think a better version could:

  • Let the caller pick a time window (for example, 6 to 8 p.m.).
  • Say up front how long the callback is likely to take.
  • Count the callback wait in the published wait-time number.

It wouldn’t fix everything. It might help more people actually get through, and I’d like to learn what people who run these phone lines think of it.

Sources

  • Social Security Administration Office of the Inspector General, “Social Security Administration’s Telephone Metrics” (FY 2025 wait, callback and abandon times, and how callbacks are counted)
  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, “Employee Benefits in the United States, March 2026,” Table 6, paid sick leave access by wage group
  • NPR, interview with Annie Lowrey about The Time Tax (Aug 31, 2026; “time tax” definition and the Wisconsin 99.5% claim)

This post is my argument, not a research finding. I’m a student sharing what I’m learning, and this isn’t legal or benefits advice.

item.title: What the Black Panthers and Dr. King both saw about poverty
item.description: Why I think the Black Panther Party and Martin Luther King Jr. belong in one story: free breakfast, a guaranteed income, why the FBI went after both, and what I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
A look at the Black Panther Party and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. side by side. They disagreed about a lot, and putting them in one story is my own reading. I’m not speaking for either of them.

Two stories we usually keep apart

Most of us get taught these as two opposite stories. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. is the peaceful dreamer. The Black Panther Party is the angry young men with guns.

The more I read, the more I think that split hides what they had in common. I’m still learning, and I could be wrong about parts of this.

They really did disagree. King believed in nonviolence his whole life. The Panthers, started by Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale in Oakland in October 1966, believed in armed self-defense. I don’t want to blur that.

But by the late 1960s, both had landed on the same problem. It was poverty, and who the country was willing to leave hungry.

Breakfast as a revolution

In January 1969, the Panthers started serving free breakfast to kids at St. Augustine’s Episcopal Church in West Oakland. The idea was simple. Kids can’t learn when they’re hungry.

The program spread to Panther chapters in other cities that same year. The Party added free health clinics and testing for sickle cell anemia, a disease that hit Black families hard and got little attention from doctors. The sociologist Alondra Nelson wrote a whole book about this work, called Body and Soul.

The Panthers called these survival programs. What feels revolutionary to me is who did the work. Neighbors fed neighbors, and every bowl of cereal showed what the government wasn’t doing.

King’s turn toward the economy

King’s last years usually get skipped. In his 1967 book Where Do We Go from Here: Chaos or Community?, he wrote that “the solution to poverty is to abolish it directly by a now widely discussed measure: the guaranteed income.”

That April, at Riverside Church in New York, he named what he called the “giant triplets of racism, extreme materialism, and militarism.” Then he began planning the Poor People’s Campaign. The plan was to bring poor people of every race to Washington to demand jobs and an income.

In the spring of 1968, he went to Memphis to stand with Black sanitation workers on strike. They carried signs that said “I AM A MAN.” King was killed there on April 4, 1968.

The campaign went on without him. That May, thousands of people camped on the National Mall in a tent city they called Resurrection City.

The FBI saw it before most people did

This is the part that makes me angry. Under J. Edgar Hoover, the FBI ran a secret program called COINTELPRO. The FBI wiretapped King, and in 1964 it mailed him an anonymous letter that his staff read as urging him to kill himself.

The FBI also wrote that it wanted to stop the rise of a “messiah” who could unify Black Americans. It named King as a possible one.

In September 1968, Hoover called the Black Panther Party “the greatest threat to the internal security of the country.” The next July, FBI headquarters wrote to its San Francisco office that the breakfast program was “a potentially successful effort by the BPP to teach children to hate police.” The FBI was scared of free breakfast.

In December 1969, police raided the Chicago apartment of Fred Hampton, the 21-year-old leader of the Illinois Panthers, and killed him in his bed. An FBI informant had given them a floor plan of the apartment.

Hampton had built what he called a Rainbow Coalition with the Young Lords, a Puerto Rican group, and the Young Patriots, poor white Southerners living in Chicago. Poor people of every color working together was the same thing King was trying to build with the Poor People’s Campaign. I think that’s why both scared the people in power.

How we found out

In March 1971, a small group of people broke into an FBI office in Media, Pennsylvania, just outside Philadelphia. They mailed the files to reporters. One file had a word most of the public had never seen: COINTELPRO.

In 1975 and 1976, a Senate committee led by Frank Church laid out what the FBI had done. It’s hard for me to read. It also gives me some hope, because ordinary people near my hometown are the reason we know.

Why I think it was one of the greatest revolutions

Neither one won everything it fought for. Poverty is still here, and I don’t want to pretend otherwise.

But I think they changed what a lot of people believe they’re owed. The government started the School Breakfast Program as a pilot in 1966 and made it permanent in 1975. I can’t say the Panthers caused that, and I don’t want to claim more than the history shows. I do think they made hungry kids much harder to ignore.

To me, a revolution is a change in what ordinary people expect from each other and from their country. King gave a lot of people the words for that. The Panthers showed what it looked like on a Tuesday morning before school.

What I’m trying

Both of them started with a need right in front of them. Here’s what I’m trying, and you’re welcome to try it with me.

One. I’m reading this history with friends in a reading circle. The Young Lords are on our list.

Two. I’m looking for one need in my own city that neighbors could meet together. If you’re in Philly, I keep a list of places to start.

Three. I’m mapping my own social location, so I can see which needs I never had to notice.

I want to keep learning from both of them, and practice noticing who’s hungry near me before I decide who’s to blame.

Sources

  • Nelson, A. (2011). Body and Soul: The Black Panther Party and the Fight against Medical Discrimination. University of Minnesota Press: survival programs, free clinics, sickle cell testing.
  • Bloom, J., & Martin, W. E. (2013). Black against Empire: The History and Politics of the Black Panther Party. University of California Press: the 1966 founding and the breakfast program’s start and spread in 1969.
  • U.S. Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities (Church Committee). (1976). Final Report, Book III: COINTELPRO, Hoover’s September 1968 statement, the July 1969 breakfast program memo, and the FBI’s campaign against King.
  • Stanford University, Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute. “Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)”: the wiretaps, the 1964 letter, and the “messiah” goal.
  • King, M. L., Jr. (1967). Where Do We Go from Here: Chaos or Community? Harper & Row: the guaranteed income quote.
  • King, M. L., Jr. (1967, April 4). “Beyond Vietnam: A Time to Break Silence.” Riverside Church, New York: the “giant triplets” quote.
  • Haas, J. (2010). The Assassination of Fred Hampton. Lawrence Hill Books: the raid, the informant’s floor plan, and the Rainbow Coalition.
  • Medsger, B. (2014). The Burglary: The Discovery of J. Edgar Hoover’s Secret FBI. Knopf: the 1971 break-in in Media, Pennsylvania.
  • USDA Food and Nutrition Service. “School Breakfast Program: Program History”: the 1966 pilot and 1975 permanent authorization.

item.title: Why I think everyone should try therapy
item.description: Why I think everyone should try therapy at least once, what surprised me in school, and three things I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script I read for one of my TikTok videos. I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

Why I believe this

I think everyone should try therapy at least once. This one’s personal, so here’s why.

I’m a therapy grad student, and I’m still learning. So this is just me sharing what I believe.

I grew up in Philadelphia and moved to San Diego.

Therapists go too

Something that surprised me in school is that most therapists have been to therapy themselves. The American Psychological Association says about three out of four mental health professionals have. The people who know it best keep choosing it.

It also doesn’t have to take forever. The APA points to a classic study where half of people improved after eight sessions, and 75 percent improved after six months.

What gets in the way

A lot of us learned that therapy means something is wrong with you. I understand where that comes from. Many families were just trying to survive, and there wasn’t time or money to talk about feelings.

You don’t need a crisis to go. You can go because you’re stressed, grieving, stuck in the same argument, or you just want to know yourself better.

It also costs money and time, and I wish it were easier for everyone to get.

Making therapy feel normal

Here are three things I’m trying.

One. I say the word “therapy” out loud with friends and family, so it feels normal.

Two. When cost is the problem, I ask about sliding scale fees, community clinics, and university training clinics.

Three. I treat a first session like a first conversation. If it doesn’t feel like a fit, it’s okay to try someone else.

If you’re in crisis right now, you can call or text 988 in the U.S.

What’s one thing that has kept you from trying therapy?

Check it yourself

  • American Psychological Association, “Understanding psychotherapy and how it works” (2023)
  • APA Monitor on Psychology, “CE Corner,” April 2014
  • Howard, K. I., Kopta, S. M., Krause, M. S., & Orlinsky, D. E. (1986). The dose-effect relationship in psychotherapy. American Psychologist, 41(2), 159-164.

Student writing, not clinical advice. If you are struggling, a licensed professional or a local crisis line can help.

item.title: Why so many of us feel lonely
item.description: What the Surgeon General's report on loneliness found, what couples therapy says about needing people, and three things I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script from my video series “Things therapy school taught me about society.” I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

How lonely we are

About half of American adults say they’ve felt lonely. In therapy school, I learned that says a lot about how we live, and less about who we are.

I’m a therapy grad student, and I’m still learning. So take this as me thinking out loud.

In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General, Dr. Vivek Murthy, put out a report called Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation. It said being disconnected can be as hard on your health as smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.

It also found that in 2020, Americans spent about 20 minutes a day in person with friends. Nearly twenty years earlier, it was about an hour. For people 15 to 24, time with friends dropped about 70 percent.

2020 was a pandemic year, so keep that in mind. It’s still a big drop.

We’re built to lean on each other

One idea from couples therapy I keep thinking about comes from Dr. Sue Johnson. With Les Greenberg, she developed Emotionally Focused Therapy. It’s built on attachment theory from the psychiatrist John Bowlby.

The idea is that needing other people is how humans are built. Leaning on someone is healthy.

One study shows it. In 2006, James Coan and his team put 16 married women in a brain scanner and told them they might get an electric shock. Holding their husband’s hand calmed the threat response in their brains.

A stranger’s hand helped too, just less. And the happier the marriage, the calmer some of those areas got.

Why it gets treated like a flaw

So when we tell people to handle everything alone, we’re asking them to go against how they’re wired. A lot of us grew up hearing “don’t be a burden.” We move away for school or work. We say “I’m fine” when we’re not.

It frustrates me that we treat loneliness like a personal flaw. But I have hope, because connection is something we can practice. I see people do it every day, like the neighbor who waves, or the friend who texts “thinking of you.”

Small ways to reach out

Here are three things I’m trying.

One. Text one person just to say I’m thinking of them.

Two. When I’m struggling, tell one person the truth before I say “I’m fine.”

Three. Say yes to one small in-person thing this week, even when staying home is easier.

Who’s someone you could reach out to today?

Check it yourself

  • U.S. Surgeon General, Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation (2023)
  • PBS NewsHour, “Loneliness poses health risks as deadly as smoking, U.S. surgeon general says” (2023)
  • Coan, J. A., Schaefer, H. S., & Davidson, R. J. (2006). Lending a hand. Psychological Science, 17(12), 1032-1039 (PubMed)
  • Boston Globe obituary for Sue Johnson (May 29, 2024)

item.title: What fights are really asking
item.description: What Emotionally Focused Therapy taught me about fights: why many fights are a protest, the negative cycle, what's under the anger, and three things I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script from my video series “Things therapy school taught me about society.” I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

The question under the fight

When someone you love yells about the dishes, they might be asking a totally different question. Therapy school taught me what that question is.

I’m a therapy grad student, and I’m still learning. So take this as me thinking out loud.

In 1985, Dr. Sue Johnson and Dr. Les Greenberg first tested something called Emotionally Focused Therapy, or EFT. Johnson centered it on attachment theory, the idea that we all need to feel safe with the people closest to us.

Johnson saw a lot of fights as a kind of protest. Underneath the fight about dishes or money, someone is asking, “Are you there for me? Do I matter to you?”

The cycle couples get stuck in

When that question doesn’t get answered, couples fall into a pattern. One person pushes and criticizes. The other shuts down to keep the peace.

The more one pushes, the more the other pulls away. EFT calls this the negative cycle. It treats the cycle as the enemy, instead of either person.

How EFT helps

In EFT, therapists help people find what’s under the anger. Often it’s hurt, fear, shame or longing.

EFT works in three stages. First, slow the cycle down and name it together. Second, share those softer feelings and learn to answer each other. Third, practice the new way until it feels normal.

Early studies found about 7 in 10 couples were no longer in distress a few months after EFT. Those studies were small, and some researchers have questioned them, so I hold that loosely.

The same loop everywhere

What stays with me is how much this fits the rest of life. When someone sounds angry at work, in our families or online, we react to the loudest part. We argue back or we tune them out.

Then they get louder, and we pull away more. It’s the same cycle, just bigger.

It frustrates me how fast we write people off as “too much.” But I have hope, because I see people slow down and get curious about each other every day.

Getting out of the loop

Here are three things I’m trying.

One. When someone snaps at me, I ask myself what they might be hurt or scared about.

Two. When I’m angry, I try to say the softer feeling underneath, like “I felt left out.”

Three. When a fight keeps repeating, I name the pattern instead of blaming the person. Something like, “We’re in that loop again.”

What do you think your last argument was really asking?

Check it yourself

  • ICEEFT, Johnson and Greenberg (1985) outcome study
  • ICEEFT, Johnson, Hunsley, Greenberg and Schindler (1999), “Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy: Status and Challenges”
  • Simply Psychology, “Emotionally Focused Therapy for Couples”
  • Wikipedia, “Emotionally focused therapy” (includes James Coyne’s 2014 critique of the early studies)
  • EFT isn’t meant for relationships with ongoing abuse or violence.

item.title: Who was your secure base? What attachment theory taught me
item.description: What attachment theory says about love: Bowlby's report, Ainsworth's Strange Situation, the love quiz, earned security, the feminist critique, and three things I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script from my video series “Things therapy school taught me about society.” I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

Where attachment theory came from

Before you could even talk, you were already learning if people would show up for you. Therapy school taught me how much that follows us, and how much society shapes it.

I’m a therapy grad student, and I’m still learning. So take this as me thinking out loud.

After World War II, the World Health Organization asked a British psychiatrist named John Bowlby to study children who had lost their homes and families. His 1951 report helped start what we now call attachment theory. The idea is that kids need at least one warm, steady person to feel safe with.

Later, psychologist Mary Ainsworth in Baltimore built a lab test called the Strange Situation. A parent leaves the room for a few minutes, then comes back. In her early studies, about 7 in 10 babies were upset when the parent left and easy to comfort when they came back. She called that secure.

Researchers call that parent a secure base. It’s the person you explore the world from, and come back to when you’re scared.

How adults love

In 1987, Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver put a love quiz in a newspaper. About 620 people answered, and the same kinds of patterns showed up in how adults love. Some feel safe getting close.

Some keep their distance. Some worry a lot about being left.

It can change

The part that gives me hope is that it can change. In one study that followed people from birth, some kids who weren’t secure as babies grew up secure. Researchers call it earned security. Their relationships as young adults looked about as healthy as people who were secure all along.

More than mothers

Here’s what frustrates me. Bowlby’s early work put almost all of it on mothers. Later researchers like Michael Rutter pushed back, and feminist critics pointed out that kids are raised by a lot of people.

Bowlby himself wrote, “If a community values its children it must cherish its parents.” To me that means a parent who’s stressed and alone needs support too.

Being a steady person

Here are three things I’m trying.

One. When I get close to someone, I notice my pattern. Do I pull away, or hold on tighter?

Two. I try to be a steady person for someone, in small ways, like showing up when I said I would.

Three. I check on the parents and caregivers around me, and ask what would actually help.

Who was a secure base for you?

Check it yourself

  • Bowlby, J. (1951). Maternal Care and Mental Health. World Health Organization (Milbank Quarterly copy)
  • Attachment Project, “Mary Ainsworth”
  • Hazan, C., & Shaver, P. (1987). Romantic love conceptualized as an attachment process. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 52(3), 511-524.
  • Roisman, G. I., Padrón, E., Sroufe, L. A., & Egeland, B. (2002). Earned-secure attachment status in retrospect and prospect. Child Development, 73(4), 1204-1219.
  • Wikipedia, “Maternal deprivation” (Rutter and the feminist critique)

item.title: Why mental health matters
item.description: Half of mental health conditions start by age 14, many people wait years for help, and three things I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script I read for one of my TikTok videos. I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

When it starts

Half of all mental health conditions start by age 14. And a lot of people wait years before they ever get help.

I’m a therapy grad student, and I’m still learning. So take this as me thinking out loud.

In 2005, Ronald Kessler and his team looked at a big national survey in the U.S. They found that half of all lifetime cases started by age 14, and three out of four started by age 24.

The same team looked at how long people waited. Among people who did get help, the wait was 6 to 8 years for depression and other mood conditions. For anxiety, it was 9 to 23 years.

That can be a whole childhood. Sometimes a whole young adulthood.

How common it is

And it’s common. The World Health Organization says about 1 in 8 people in the world were living with a mental health condition in 2019. In the U.S. in 2022, it was almost 1 in 4 adults, and only about half of them got treatment that year.

The WHO calls mental health an integral part of our general health. I think about that a lot. We wouldn’t tell someone to wait nine years to get a broken arm looked at.

Why people wait

It makes me angry that so many people carry this for years. A lot of it comes from shame, from cost, and from families who never had the words for it. I understand why. Many families were just trying to survive.

But I have hope, because I see it changing. The friend who asks a second time. The teacher who notices. The family that starts saying the word “therapy” out loud.

Talking about it plainly

Here are three things I’m trying.

One. Ask “how are you, really?” and actually wait for the answer.

Two. Talk about mental health the way I’d talk about a sore back, plainly and without shame.

Three. Keep 988 saved in my phone. If you or someone you love is in crisis, you can call or text 988 in the U.S.

What’s one thing you wish someone had told you about mental health when you were 14?

Check it yourself

  • Kessler, R. C., et al. (2005). Lifetime prevalence and age-of-onset distributions of DSM-IV disorders in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication. Archives of General Psychiatry, 62(6), 593-602.
  • Wang, P. S., et al. (2005). Failure and delay in initial treatment contact after first onset of mental disorders. Archives of General Psychiatry, 62(6), 603-613.
  • World Health Organization, World Mental Health Report (2022)

item.title: Learning how to apologize, and how to move on
item.description: What couples research and restorative justice taught me about apologizing, guilt versus shame, and letting myself move on.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script I read for one of my TikTok videos. I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

Why repair matters

Nobody taught me how to apologize. And nobody taught me how to move on after.

I’m in therapy school, and I’m still bad at both. But here’s what I’ve been learning.

A psychologist named John Gottman studied couples for decades. The couples who lasted still fought. The difference was they repaired. Even babies and parents fall out of sync all the time, and researchers found that the repair is how trust gets built.

Guilt and shame

So why is it so hard? Brené Brown says guilt sounds like “I did something bad.” Shame sounds like “I am bad.”

Guilt can help us change. Shame makes us hide, or blame someone else.

A society that runs on shame

And our society runs on shame. One mistake can follow you forever online. Our justice system mostly asks how to punish someone.

Restorative justice asks different questions: Who was hurt? What do they need? Whose job is it to make it right?

That makes me angry, because people can grow when we give them a way back.

How I’m practicing sorry

Here are three things I’m trying.

One. Say sorry without a “but.” Name what I did and how it landed.

Two. Ask what would help make it right, and then actually do it.

Three. Once I’ve done my part, let myself move on. It still mattered. I just want to carry the lesson forward and leave the shame behind.

What did your family teach you about saying sorry?

item.title: Why we blame the person instead of the situation
item.description: Why we judge others harder than ourselves: the Castro essays, the Good Samaritan study, how culture shapes blame, and three things I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script from my video series “Things therapy school taught me about society.” I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

A name for the habit

Someone cuts you off in traffic, and your first thought is “what a jerk.” When you cut someone off, it’s because you’re running late. Psychologists have a name for that.

I’m a therapy grad student, and I’m still learning. So take this as me thinking out loud.

In 1977, the psychologist Lee Ross called it the fundamental attribution error. We tend to explain other people’s actions by who they are, and we forget the situation they’re in.

What the studies found

You can see it in a study from 1967. People read essays praising Fidel Castro. Even when they were told a coin toss decided what the writer had to argue, they still guessed the writer liked Castro.

In 1973, researchers at Princeton asked seminary students to walk to another building and give a talk. Some of them were about to talk about the Good Samaritan. On the way, they passed a man slumped in a doorway. When they weren’t in a hurry, 63 percent stopped to help.

When they were told they were late, only 10 percent did. Their talk topic barely made a difference. The hurry did.

Some of this is learned. In 1984, Joan Miller compared Americans and Hindus in India. The older people got, the more Americans explained behavior by personality, and the more Indians pointed to the situation.

Why it matters

This matters because when we only see the person, we blame them. Someone’s late to work. Someone can’t pay rent.

A kid acts out in class. In therapy school, we learn to ask what’s happening around a person before we ask what’s wrong with them.

It frustrates me how fast my brain jumps to blame. But I have hope, because it’s a habit, and habits can change. I see people do it every day, like the coworker who asks if you’re okay before getting mad, or the teacher who asks what’s going on at home.

Looking at the situation first

Here are three things I’m trying.

One. When someone annoys me, I think of one situation that could explain it before I decide who they are.

Two. Ask “what’s going on?” before “what’s wrong with you?”

Three. Give other people the same grace I give myself on a bad day.

When’s a time someone gave you the benefit of the doubt?

Check it yourself

item.title: How competition wears down the people at the bottom
item.description: Survival of the fittest, Adam Smith's sympathy, the Matthew effect, the Whitehall study, mutual aid, and three things I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script from my video series “Things therapy school taught me about society.” I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

The race we’re told to run

We’re told competition makes everyone better. So why does it keep wearing down the people at the bottom?

I’m a therapy grad student, and I’m still learning. So take this as me thinking out loud.

In 1864, a philosopher named Herbert Spencer coined the phrase “survival of the fittest.” People took it and said the rich deserve to win and the poor deserve to lose. That idea stuck. Companies compete for profit, workers compete for jobs, and kids compete for spots in good schools.

I want to be fair. Competition can push prices down. Adam Smith wrote about that in 1776. Seventeen years earlier, he wrote a whole book on sympathy, which people tend to forget.

Who starts ahead

The problem is who starts the race ahead. In 1968, the sociologist Robert Merton named the Matthew effect, after a line in the Gospel of Matthew. He saw that famous scientists got more credit than unknown ones for similar work.

People have since seen the same pattern everywhere. The people who have more get more, and a head start turns into a bigger head start.

What losing costs

Losing the race costs your body and your mind. Starting in 1967, the Whitehall study followed about 17,000 British civil servants. The lower the job rank, the higher the death rate.

The men at the bottom died of heart disease at more than three times the rate of the men at the top, even after counting smoking, blood pressure, and cholesterol. In 2013, researchers found that when people with low incomes thought about money problems, their thinking dropped about as much as losing a full night of sleep.

In therapy school, we learn to look at the stress around a person before we blame the person. Being at the bottom of a race you didn’t choose is stressful.

Working together

That makes me angry. But I have hope. In 1902, Peter Kropotkin wrote that mutual aid is “as much a law of nature as mutual struggle.”

He saw animals and people survive by working together. You can see it today in credit unions, co-ops, tenant unions, and neighbors sharing rides and childcare.

Getting on the same team

Here are three things I’m trying.

One. Notice when I’m treating someone like competition, and ask if we could be on the same team.

Two. Share what I know, like a job lead or a study guide, with someone who didn’t get the head start.

Three. Move some of my money somewhere cooperative, like a credit union or a local co-op.

Where in your life do you feel like you’re always competing?

Check it yourself

  • Smith, A. (1759). The Theory of Moral Sentiments; (1776). The Wealth of Nations.
  • Merton, R. K. (1968). The Matthew effect in science. Science, 159(3810), 56-63.

item.title: Why therapists learn cultural humility
item.description: Some history first: the Tuskegee study, cultural competence, two doctors in Oakland who offered the word humility, and three things I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script from my video series “Things therapy school taught me about society.” I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

Something I learned in therapy school that changed how I see the world. Part four. This one’s a little longer, because the history matters.

A history of mistrust

For a long time, American medicine and mental health care were built by and for a narrow group of people. From 1932 to 1972, the U.S. Public Health Service ran the Tuskegee study. Hundreds of Black men with syphilis were watched and left untreated, even after penicillin became the standard cure.

Stories like that are part of why many communities still have good reasons to be careful with doctors and therapists.

The first fix

By the late 1980s, people in the field were pushing for change. In 1989, Terry Cross and his colleagues wrote about cultural competence. The idea was that care systems should learn to work well with people from every culture.

It was a real step forward. In practice, though, it sometimes turned into a checklist. Learn five facts about a culture, and you’re competent.

Two doctors in Oakland

In 1998, Melanie Tervalon and Jann Murray-García, who trained doctors at Children’s Hospital Oakland, offered a different word. Humility.

They described cultural humility as a lifelong practice. You keep checking your own assumptions. You notice the power you hold in the room. And you build real partnerships with the communities you serve.

The shift looks small on paper. You stop treating culture as something you can finish learning.

Outside the therapy room

When I learned this, I noticed how often I act like I’ve finished learning about other people. I read one article, or I know one person, and I decide I get it. Cultural humility asks for something slower. It asks me to stay curious.

I’m still working on this. Here are three things I’m trying.

One. When I meet someone from a culture I don’t know well, I ask before I assume.

Two. When I’m the one with more power in a room, like the degree or the title, I try to listen more than I talk.

Three. I learn a community’s history from people in it, through their own writers and organizers.

Check it yourself

item.title: Socialism starts with culture: Philadelphia
item.description: Why I think neighbors practice sharing before a country votes for it, Gramsci's war of position, and what Philly has shared since 1731.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script I read for one of my TikTok videos. I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

Practice before politics

Before a country votes for something like socialism, I think neighbors have to practice it first. And I want to start with the city I grew up in, Philadelphia.

As I understand it, socialism means the people who do the work and live with the results get a real say over the things that shape their lives, like housing, work, and care. I know the word scares a lot of people, including many Vietnamese families who left after 1975. I’m still learning, and I could be wrong about parts of this.

Gramsci’s idea

In the 1930s, writing from a prison cell, Antonio Gramsci asked why working people didn’t push for change even when they were struggling. Part of his answer was culture. The ideas that feel like common sense, like “everyone for themselves,” hold a system in place as strongly as any law.

Gramsci called the slow work of changing that common sense a war of position. It happens in schools, churches, families, and on the block, long before it shows up in an election.

Philly already does this

Philly has been practicing this for a long time. In 1731, Ben Franklin and his friends started a lending library so people could share books none of them could afford alone. In 1736, he helped organize a volunteer fire company. Today you can see it in Weavers Way, a member-owned grocery co-op started in 1973, and in the block captains who organize cleanups and block parties.

We just don’t always give it a name.

Starting on my block

I’m still figuring out what this looks like in my own life. Here are three things I’m trying.

One. Use what we already share, like the library, the rec center, and the park, and show up when they’re on the city budget.

Two. When I can, buy from places owned by the people who work or shop there, like a co-op.

Three. Know my block. Learn my neighbors’ names, and ask what the block needs before I decide what it needs.

I want to practice these where I’m from first, and see what grows.

item.title: Who raises a kid? Bronfenbrenner's circles
item.description: Urie Bronfenbrenner's map of everything that raises a kid, what it changed about how I think about blame, and three things I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script from my video series “Things therapy school taught me about society.” I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

Bronfenbrenner’s circles

Something I learned in therapy school that changed how I see the world. Part three.

A psychologist named Urie Bronfenbrenner drew a map of everything that raises a kid. He pictured it as circles. In the middle is the child. Around them are family, friends, and school.

Then come the things a kid never sees, like a parent’s job, the neighborhood, and local government. On the outside are the culture and the laws everyone lives under.

Rethinking blame

When I learned this, it changed how I think about blame. When a kid struggles, we usually look at the parents first. Bronfenbrenner’s map asks us to look at every circle. A parent can do everything they can and still be up against low wages, an underfunded school, or a two-hour bus ride to work.

Seeing every circle

I’m still learning to see all the circles. Here are three things I’m trying.

One. When a kid is struggling, I ask about every circle around them, beyond the home.

Two. I notice which circles I’m part of, as a neighbor, a coworker, or a voter.

Three. I pick one outer circle to show up for, like a school board meeting or a local budget hearing.

Check it yourself

item.title: The person is not the problem: what narrative therapy taught me
item.description: Michael White and David Epston's narrative therapy, how it changed the way I talk about homelessness, and three things I'm trying.

The problem is the problem

Something I learned in therapy school that changed how I see the world. Part two.

In narrative therapy, Michael White and David Epston taught a simple idea. The person is not the problem. The problem is the problem.

So a therapist might talk about “the worry” or “the anger” as something that shows up in a person’s life. That gives people room to step back from the problem and push against it together.

How we talk about homelessness

When I learned this, I thought about how we talk about people without housing. We say “the homeless,” like it’s who they are. Losing housing is something that happens to people. Rent goes up, a job ends, a hospital bill comes.

Changing how I talk

I’m still catching myself on this. Here are three things I’m trying.

One. I say “people experiencing homelessness,” or I use someone’s name if I know it.

Two. When I hear a story about someone on the street, I ask what happened before, like a rent increase or an eviction.

Three. I look up one local group that helps with housing and see what they need.

item.title: The identified patient: what one struggling kid can be carrying
item.description: The family therapy idea of the identified patient, where I see it outside the therapy room, and three things I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script from my video series “Things therapy school taught me about society.” I wrote it with AI help from published sources, checked the facts, and recorded it in my own voice. What I said on camera may differ a little.

The one the family brings in

Something I learned in therapy school that changed how I see the world. Part one.

In family therapy, there’s a term called the identified patient. It’s the one person a family brings in as the problem. A lot of the time it’s a kid. The kid who yells, skips class, or won’t listen.

Family therapists are trained to ask a different question. What is this kid carrying for everyone else? Sometimes the acting out is the loudest sign that the whole house is under stress. Money, a parent working nights, a loss nobody talks about.

Outside the therapy room

Once I learned this, I started seeing it outside the therapy room. Schools do it. News stories do it. We point at one kid, one family, or one group and call them the problem, and we skip asking what they’re carrying.

Looking at the pressure first

I’m still working on this myself. Here are three things I’m trying.

One. When someone gets called the problem, I ask what’s going on around them before I judge.

Two. I look at the pressure first, like rent, work hours, and school funding.

Three. When I talk about a group in the news, I try to name the system around them too.

Check it yourself

Everyone thinks

Some of the smartest people in your city will never be called intellectuals. Here’s why that matters.

In the 1930s, writing from a prison cell, Antonio Gramsci argued that everyone thinks, but only some people are given the title of thinker.

Patricia Hill Collins, a Black feminist scholar, took it further. She showed that Black women have long built knowledge in families, churches, and community work, even when universities didn’t call it theory.

Thinkers in your city

Today that looks like the tenant organizer who knows the housing code by heart, or the mother who has read every school board policy. Their work is often unpaid and uncredited.

Crediting the people who do the work

Here are three steps I’m trying to take.

One. Pick one issue where you live.

Two. Find who’s already organizing around it, and notice whose work goes unnamed.

Three. Ask what they need, take on one task, and credit the people who taught you.

I’m a grad student, still learning to listen first. Tell me whose work in your community deserves more credit.

item.title: My parents never had a word for it: intergenerational trauma
item.description: Intergenerational trauma as a Vietnamese American: the rules of my house, why they made sense, and three things I'm trying.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script for one of my TikTok videos. Most of the words come from my own writing and messages. AI helped me organize them and wrote a few connecting lines, and the video uses an AI voice (ElevenLabs) reading them.

What my family carried

My parents never had a word for it. They just kept going.

After 1975, many Vietnamese families left everything behind. Almost 800,000 people who escaped by boat reached other countries. Many others didn’t make it.

My family came to the United States with the immigrant mindset of survival and sacrifice. My grandparents had to survive. My mom and dad had to survive.

How it gets passed down

Here’s something I’ve been learning in school. When a family lives through that much, the pain doesn’t always get talked about. It can still get passed down. It shows up in the rules of the house.

In my house, the rules were simple. Keep your head down. Don’t complain.

Emotions were seen as a distraction from perseverance. There was love, but it showed through actions, not conversations.

Those rules helped my family survive. I understand that now. They also made me independent, and emotionally guarded. I still catch myself worrying about disappointing professors, the way I used to worry about disappointing my parents.

I’m not the only one

I don’t think I’m the only one. The U.S. Office of Minority Health says Asian Americans are 60% less likely than white Americans to get mental health services. A lot of us were taught to handle it alone.

Learning to talk about it

So here are three things I’m trying, if you want to try them with me.

One. I’m giving it a name. When I call it intergenerational trauma, I can see a pattern that started long before me.

Two. I’m asking my family small questions about their lives, and then I just listen. Parenting isn’t easy, and it was their first time too.

Three. I’m getting support. Some therapists speak Vietnamese, and some offer sliding scale fees. If it ever feels like too much, you can call or text 988.

My mom had to survive. I have the privilege to reflect. I think resilience is inherited, but it has to be redefined with each generation.

I want to be part of the generation that talks about it.

item.title: Somewhere to put it: what society owes kids with nowhere to go
item.description: Why so many kids have nowhere to put their anger: who public space is for, how Bronx kids invented hip hop as their own outlet, and what we choose to pay for.
item.content:encoded:
Where is a kid supposed to put the anger?

I keep coming back to two groups of kids. Some get pulled into crime. Some live with ghosts: a friend who died, a parent who left or was taken away, a night they keep replaying. Often they're the same kids.

My first answer was simple. Give them somewhere to go. A skate park that stays open at night.

A wall where graffiti is allowed. A breakdance circle, a rap battle, a gym that teaches defense instead of offense. A church, a temple, a cushion to meditate on.

The longer I sat with that list, the more it looked like a question about society. Why do so many kids have nowhere to put what they carry? Who decided that? And what does it say about us that when kids invent their own outlets, we so often treat the outlet as the crime?

I'm training to become a marriage and family therapist. This is a student working through research and philosophy. It isn't a program design, and it isn't advice.

A city with no room for teenagers

Look at where a teenager without money is allowed to be. The mall wants customers. The coffee shop wants a purchase.

The plaza has metal knobs bolted to its ledges so nobody can skate them. The park closes at dusk.

The sociologist Ray Oldenburg wrote about “third places,” the spots outside home and work where people gather and belong. For adults those places mostly cost money. For kids without it, the third place is the street, and the street is where they get told to move along.

The French philosopher Henri Lefebvre called this a question of the “right to the city”: the right to shape a city and use it, along with the right to visit it. The architectural historian Iain Borden argues that skateboarders make that claim with their bodies. They take a handrail built for one purpose and use it for another.

Skating is a small argument about who public space is for. Our usual answer, through skate stoppers, loitering rules, and curfews, is that it isn't for them.

Curfews show how much that answer is about how things look. A 2016 Campbell systematic review by Wilson and colleagues looked at 12 evaluations and concluded that juvenile curfews do not reduce crime or victimization. Crime during curfew hours even rose slightly.

Meanwhile, federal data have long shown that on school days, violent crime by juveniles peaks between 3 and 4 in the afternoon, right after the bell. On non-school days it peaks in the evening (Snyder & Sickmund, 1999). We keep trying to clear kids off the streets at midnight, when the clearer problem is the empty hours we never planned for.

The kids already built this once

Here's what struck me most. My list (graffiti, breakdancing, rap battles, a place to gather at night) isn't random. It's almost exactly the four elements of hip hop: writing, breaking, MCing, and DJing. Kids invented that list themselves, under some of the worst conditions an American city has produced.

In the late 1960s and 1970s, the South Bronx was cut apart by the Cross Bronx Expressway, hollowed out by disinvestment, and burned by waves of fires while services were pulled back. Gangs filled the gap.

Then, in December 1971, a peacemaker named Cornell “Black Benjie” Benjamin was beaten to death while trying to negotiate between gangs. His own gang, the Ghetto Brothers, chose not to retaliate. Their leader called a peace meeting at the Boys Club on Hoe Avenue, and a truce followed.

Historians like Jeff Chang credit that truce with opening the streets and parks for the parties where hip hop grew, including DJ Kool Herc’s 1973 back-to-school party on Sedgwick Avenue.

Think about what that means. Young people facing violence, poverty, and grief turned battles into dance battles, turf into crews, and insults into rhymes. They built the outlet society wouldn’t build for them.

And the city’s response to one of those elements, graffiti, was decades of crackdowns. The same art form now sells in galleries. When the kids do it on a train, it’s vandalism.

When it hangs on a wall downtown, it’s culture. The paint is the same. What changed is who holds the brush and who owns the wall.

Rage as a social signal

Part of my first idea was that kids need to get their rage out. The research complicates that. In a well known experiment, Brad Bushman (2002) had angry people hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who made them angry.

They came out angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing. Rage doesn’t drain like water from a tank.

I still think rage is also a social signal, beyond a private feeling to be managed.

Robert Merton argued in 1938 that crime grows where a society holds up the same goals for everyone (success, money, respect) while blocking the legitimate paths to them for some people. The sociologist Elijah Anderson, in Code of the Street (1999), described how in neighborhoods where people do not trust the police or the courts to protect them, toughness and the readiness to fight become a kind of protection. Much of the violence he describes is defensive. It’s about avoiding being seen as an easy target.

That reframes my phrase “defense, not offense.” Many kids are already playing defense.

The question is whether society gives them a form of defense that builds them up or one that gets them killed. Martial arts may be one answer. A 2017 meta-analysis by Harwood, Lavidor, and Rassovsky found that 11 of 12 controlled studies showed martial arts training reduced aggression in children and teens, though the authors called the research sparse.

What martial arts seem to teach is restraint, respect, and a teacher who watches. That’s different from blowing off steam.

The strongest evidence I found came from Chicago. Becoming a Man, a school-based program that helps teen boys slow down and think before reacting in heated moments, was tested in two randomized trials. Heller and colleagues (2017) reported that violent-crime arrests fell by 45 to 50 percent during the program.

The program never told boys their instincts were wrong. It helped them notice when an instinct built for a dangerous street was being used in a moment that didn’t need it.

The neighborhood is the program

An outlet alone is not enough. A 2016 meta-analysis by Spruit and colleagues, covering more than 132,000 adolescents, found no overall link between playing sports and lower delinquency.

In a Swedish study, Mahoney and Stattin (2000) found that structured activities were linked to low antisocial behavior, while unstructured hanging out with little adult guidance was linked to more. A skate park at night with nobody around is just a place. It isn’t a bond yet.

The sociologist Travis Hirschi argued in 1969 that people stay out of trouble mostly because of bonds: attachment to people, commitment to goals, involvement in activities, and belief in shared rules.

Robert Sampson and colleagues found something similar at the level of whole neighborhoods. Surveying 8,782 Chicago residents across 343 neighborhoods, they found that “collective efficacy,” trust among neighbors plus their willingness to step in for the common good, was linked to less violence. Poverty and instability seemed to raise violence largely by wearing that trust down (Sampson, Raudenbush, & Earls, 1997).

Even the physical place matters. In a randomized trial in Philadelphia, cleaning and greening vacant lots was followed by a 29 percent drop in gun violence near the lots in the poorest neighborhoods (Branas et al., 2018). Nobody gave a lecture. The block just started to look like someone cared about it.

So the outlet works when it is woven into a web of people. The skate park needs the older skater who teaches the younger one. The cypher needs its rules about respect.

The dojo needs its teacher. The people are what make the place work.

The kids who see ghosts

The sociologist Avery Gordon wrote that haunting is how past social violence makes itself felt in the present, even when official history says it’s over.

I think that is one way to understand kids who see ghosts. They are carrying grief that the wider society has not reckoned with: the friend lost to a shooting, the block that burned, the parent who is gone.

I also wrote the word fatherless in my first notes, and I want to handle it carefully, because many single parents do heroic work and most kids raised without a father never commit a crime. McLanahan, Tach, and Schneider (2013) reviewed the most careful studies and found father absence does seem to harm some outcomes, with the clearest evidence for high school graduation and social and emotional adjustment, though the effects are smaller than simpler studies suggest.

Absence also isn’t only a private family choice. By 2010, one in every 28 children in the United States had a parent behind bars, up from one in 125 about 25 years earlier (Pew Charitable Trusts, 2010). Some of the fatherlessness we blame on families was produced by policy.

Mentoring is one way to add steady adults back. In a large study of Big Brothers Big Sisters, Tierney, Grossman, and Resch (1995) found that young people matched with a mentor were 46 percent less likely to start using drugs and almost a third less likely to hit someone than kids still on the waitlist. A mentor can’t replace a parent. A mentor is one more person who shows up.

Spirit, of any kind

My notes said kids need spirituality, and that it does not matter which God. A 2001 meta-analysis by Baier and Wright reviewed 60 studies and found religious beliefs and practices had a moderate deterrent effect on crime.

I want to be careful with that. Kids who attend services differ in many ways from kids who do not, and nobody should be pushed into a faith.

Emile Durkheim offers a different way to read it. He argued that religion is, among other things, a society gathering and feeling itself as one. He called the shared rush of a crowd moving together “collective effervescence.”

A church service has it. So does a temple full of chanting, a meditation hall in silence, and, I would argue, a cypher when the whole circle reacts to one line. Maybe what kids need from spirituality has less to do with a particular God, and more to do with belonging to something larger than their anger, with people who expect them back next week.

What we choose to pay for

A 2020 report found that the average cost of the most expensive confinement option for a young person was $214,620 per year (Justice Policy Institute, cited in Sticker Shock 2020). I keep holding that number next to the empty skate park and the locked rec center. We already spend money on these kids. We just choose to spend it after the harm instead of before it.

That’s the deepest thing this question taught me. Crime by young people is partly a story about choices. It’s also a story about what a society builds, what it tears down, which spaces it opens and which ones it locks, and which kids it decides are worth investing in early.

The kids in the Bronx proved decades ago that young people will make meaning out of almost nothing. I want to learn how the rest of us can meet them halfway.

What I still don’t know

I couldn’t find solid research on night skate parks or legal graffiti walls and crime. That doesn’t prove they fail. It means nobody has measured them well.

I don’t know which outlets help which kids, or whether a night skate park with one trusted adult would look more like Becoming a Man or more like an empty youth center. I would love to see a city try it and count honestly.

If you or someone you know is struggling

In the United States, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at any hour. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911. This essay is a student reflection and does not offer therapy, legal, or medical advice.

item.title: The story my family handed me
item.description: My story in scenes: growing up Vietnamese American in Pennsylvania, moving to San Diego, a role-play in therapy school, and what's helping me.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script for one of my TikTok videos. Most of the words come from my own writing and messages. AI helped me organize them and wrote a few connecting lines, and the video uses an AI voice (ElevenLabs) reading them.

Pennsylvania

No one ever invited my parents over for dinner.

I grew up in a white suburban town in Pennsylvania, and it was isolating in many ways. No one made an effort to connect with my parents. That sense of social exclusion pushed them to stay within their Vietnamese circle.

My family came to the United States with the immigrant mindset of survival and sacrifice. My grandparents had to survive. My mom and dad had to survive. They taught us to keep our heads down and not complain.

That made me independent, but also emotionally guarded. Emotions were seen as a distraction from perseverance. There was love, but it showed through actions, not conversations.

My parents took us to parks, and we enjoyed the simple things in life.

I’ve complained about the prejudices put on me in elementary school. But when I look at my mom’s life, the racism I’ve faced is not close to what she experienced. Her motto was, “If there’s a will, there’s a way.”

Leaving

It wasn’t until I went to college and was exposed to more diversity that I began to question some of what I grew up with.

Vietnamese food became a reminder of love and connection, especially after I moved away from Philadelphia.

San Diego

Then I moved to San Diego. Meeting other Asian Americans out here was a culture shock. Things moved so much faster in California. It felt like I’d landed somewhere completely new.

Living in San Diego now, I feel more Americanized, but I still find myself pulled toward my Vietnamese roots. Living between those cultures has often left me feeling pulled in both directions.

Choosing graduate school, knowing my family had financial needs, brought both pride and guilt. I sometimes catch myself worrying about disappointing professors or supervisors, the way I used to worry about disappointing my parents.

The moment I noticed

Then something happened in my Marriage and Family Therapy training. In a role-play, I almost handed a client the advice I wished someone had given me. Her family sounded like mine. I stopped myself, but only just.

That’s when I saw it. The old story was still running. A lot of us learned to carry everything alone, and it follows you.

What’s helping me

So what’s helping me? Three things.

One. I gave the old story a name. In narrative therapy, naming a story helps you see it as something you learned. Mine is “Keep Your Head Down.”

Two. I’m learning our emotional and cultural language, and the social differences around it. In my family, love was in the food. And I’m learning how to respect their values. Parenting isn’t easy, and it was their first time too.

Three. I’m learning to say it out loud. I still work on asking for help and trusting others with my emotions.

Back at the table

I have the privilege to reflect. I think resilience is inherited, but it has to be redefined with each generation.

Healing, to me, means being able to face where you come from without letting it define you.

If I could talk to my younger self, I’d tell him it’s okay to speak up and not carry everything alone. Maybe that starts at dinner.

Check it yourself

  • Narrative therapy idea of naming a story: White, M., & Epston, D. (1990). Narrative Means to Therapeutic Ends.

item.title: Do you know the number for a mental health emergency?
item.description: 988, the free and confidential crisis line most people still haven't heard of.
item.content:encoded:
This is the script for one of my TikTok videos. I wrote it with AI help and picked the final version, and the video uses an AI voice (ElevenLabs) reading it.

A number worth knowing

Okay, quick. What number do you call for a fire? 911. Easy.

Now what do you call when your mind is the emergency?

Most people don’t know. In a 2023 survey, only 13% of U.S. adults had heard of 988.

I’m a therapy grad student, and that still gets to me. It’s free and confidential. You can call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org, 24/7.

Help like this rarely has money for ads. So it spreads the way good things usually spread. One person tells another.

So I’m telling you, and I hope you tell one more person.

item.title: Where power and identity cross: intersectionality through Foucault
item.description: A student reads Kimberlé Crenshaw's intersectionality next to Michel Foucault's ideas about power, knowledge and categories. Foucault never used the word. Putting them together is my own reading.
item.content:encoded:
A reading of Kimberlé Crenshaw's idea of intersectionality next to the work of Michel Foucault. Foucault died in 1984 and never used the word intersectionality. Putting the two together is my own reading, and I am not speaking for either of them.

On this blog I've written about social location and privilege. Both posts said the parts of who we are stack. Race, class, gender, language and immigration story pile on top of each other.

Those posts left me with a question I didn't answer. If the parts stack, who does the stacking, and where? This post is my attempt to work through it with two thinkers who never met.

Where the word comes from

Kimberlé Crenshaw is a law professor. She used the word intersectionality in a 1989 paper in the University of Chicago Legal Forum. She was building on Black feminist writers who came before her, including the Combahee River Collective, whose 1977 statement described oppressions as "interlocking."

One of the cases in her paper was DeGraffenreid v. General Motors, decided in 1976. Five Black women said GM's seniority system pushed them out during layoffs, because the company had not hired Black women before 1964. The court said they could bring a race claim or a sex claim, but would not let them combine the two.

GM had hired women before 1964. They were white women. So on the court's view, there was no sex discrimination, and the race claim was treated as a separate matter. The thing that actually happened to these women had no box to go in.

That makes me angry. Five women walked into court with a real loss, and the law's own categories were the reason they walked out with nothing.

Crenshaw's point was that some harm only shows up where the categories cross. If you look at one category at a time, you can miss it completely.

What Foucault looked at

Foucault spent much of his work on how power runs through ordinary institutions. In Discipline and Punish (1975), he wrote about prisons, schools, hospitals and the army. He showed how watching people, testing them, ranking them and keeping records on them trains them to act a certain way.

He also tied power to knowledge. Whoever gets to define what counts as normal, healthy or reasonable holds a kind of power. Over time, those definitions start to look like plain facts about people.

In The History of Sexuality, Volume 1 (1976), he argued that power comes from everywhere. It moves through many small relationships, in families, clinics and workplaces as well as governments. He also wrote that where there is power, there is resistance.

In that same book he described what he called biopower. Modern states manage whole populations through numbers like birth rates, health records and life expectancy. Counting people is one way of governing them.

Putting them side by side

Here is where the two ideas connect for me. Crenshaw shows that the categories stack. Foucault helps me ask where the categories come from and how they get kept in place.

The court in DeGraffenreid was using the categories the law already had. Race claim. Sex claim.

The court treated those boxes as if they described how people actually live. Because the knowledge was built that way, the women's experience didn't register as real.

I think the same thing can happen with numbers. If a report breaks data down by race, then by gender, then by income, one at a time, a group sitting where those cross can disappear. Nobody has to intend that. The form does it.

I also understand why systems work this way. A court has to sort claims somehow, and an office has to count people somehow. One category at a time is easier to run and easier to check. The cost is that what's simple for the system can leave a person unseen.

Where the hope is

Foucault's line about resistance is the part I hold onto. Power runs through ordinary places, and so does pushback. The women in DeGraffenreid lost their case, but their case is a big part of why Crenshaw gave this problem a name.

The Combahee River Collective were a small group of Black women in Boston who met and wrote together. Their 1977 statement still gets read today. Good keeps showing up in places like that, usually from people nobody put in charge.

There are practical fixes too. A form can leave room for someone to describe their own life in their own words. A report can look at where groups cross, like Black women or older immigrants, as well as each group alone. A person in a helping job can ask one more question before deciding they understand.

The strongest objection

Some critics argue that Foucault's picture of power is so spread out that it's hard to say who is responsible for anything. The philosopher Nancy Fraser made a version of this argument in 1981. She said Foucault describes power well but makes it hard to say which uses of power are wrong.

Crenshaw's work points at specific harms, specific courts and specific laws. So there is a real tension in reading them together. I don't think Foucault's ideas should be used to blur who made a decision. In DeGraffenreid, a real court made a real ruling.

Where I got it wrong

In my post on social location, I wrote about a training role-play where I almost handed a client the advice I wished someone had given me. Her family sounded like mine. I stopped myself, but only just.

Reading Crenshaw and Foucault together, I see one more piece of that moment. The categories I shared with her felt like knowledge about her. That feeling of already knowing is exactly where I need to slow down.

What I still don't know

How does a therapist ask about the parts of someone's life that cross, without turning the conversation into a checklist of labels? Which intake forms in my field ask about one category at a time, and what do they miss? How do I hold a pattern in mind while letting the person in front of me lead?

Where I'm going with this

I want to practice noticing when a form, a framework or my own first guess is sorting someone one category at a time. When I catch it, I want to ask what sits where those categories cross, and let the person tell me.

  • Nancy Fraser, "Foucault on Modern Power: Empirical Insights and Normative Confusions," Praxis International (1981).

item.title: Who Gets Measured, and Who Does the Measuring
item.description: A reading of two school debates, behavior scores and AI glasses at exams, through Michel Foucault's idea of the examination. My own reading, not his voice.
item.content:encoded:
A reading of two school debates through the work of Michel Foucault. The ideas below are my own reading of his book Discipline and Punish. I am not speaking for him.

Two school debates this week raised a question for me: what are we measuring, and who bears the cost of measuring it? One asked whether behavior should count toward a grade. The other asked how schools should respond to AI glasses used to cheat on exams in South Korea.

The behavior score

A behavior score converts conduct into a number, and that number travels with the student. Someone has to define what good behavior looks like. One commenter noted that such scores can disadvantage boys and autistic girls, and I think that deserves attention. A definition of "well behaved" tends to favor the students who already fit it.

A second problem is practical. When a grade blends mastery with compliance, a reader cannot tell what a 90 means. Separating the two at least makes clear what each number measures.

The U.S. Department of Education's January 2025 First Look report on 2021–22 civil-rights data found that students with disabilities made up 17% of K–12 enrollment and 29% of students who received one or more out-of-school suspensions. That is a disciplinary measure, not evidence about behavior grades, but it gives me reason to ask whether adults' judgments about behavior are applied evenly.

At the same time, schools need shared rules, and a clear behavior score may tell students what is expected and give teachers a way to recognize cooperation or effort. Schools may also argue that recording behavior helps them respond when disruptions affect classmates' ability to learn.

The exam

In Discipline and Punish, Foucault describes the examination as a tool that observes people and ranks them in the same act. The glasses case shows how far that observation has to stretch once the technology becomes small enough to hide. Replies in the thread showed the cost.

Oral checks and in-class work take teacher time. Device inspections take proctor time.

I do not think there is a clean answer. A more useful question may be which parts of an exam truly require close watching, and which could become a conversation about the student's thinking.

What I still don't know

How can a student challenge a behavior score or explain what happened? Where should a school draw the line between noticing a pattern and monitoring every action?

Why I am writing about this

Foucault asked how institutions decide what counts as normal, and what that decision costs the people inside them. That question applies well beyond school. I plan to keep asking it here, in plain language, and to say clearly when I am unsure.

Nick writes at hoto.lol. AI helped build this site because I need accessibility support.
