item.title: Fearless speech for regular people: parrhesia meets boundary scripts
item.description: Foucault's idea of parrhesia, what it is not, and four short boundary sentences for work and family.
item.content:encoded:
What does it mean to speak truthfully when the person listening has power over what happens next?

Foucault's fearless speech is serious, useful, and easy to misuse. His last lectures gave a name to courage that has little to do with shouting. I am learning how much risk and honesty his definition demands.

In his first The Courage of Truth lecture, dated February 1, 1984, Foucault ties parrhesia to the speaker's conviction and the risk to the listener relationship. Read the transcript.

He called it parrhesia

The word comes from ancient Greek. It means roughly “saying everything,” or speaking the whole truth out loud. Foucault followed the idea through Euripides, the Cynics, and the Roman Stoics.

He covered it in two lecture courses. The Government of Self and Others (1983) and The Courage of Truth (1984) were those courses. Berkeley talks later collected as Fearless Speech covered the idea too.

His definition has three parts, and all three need to be there.

First, the speaker believes what they say. Their words express their own conviction, without a handed-down talking point.

Second, speaking carries risk. A person might lose status, a job, a relationship, or someone's good opinion. When speaking costs nothing, Foucault would not call it parrhesia. He was blunt about the parrhesiastes risking the relationship itself to tell the truth.

Third, the truth goes to someone who could hurt the speaker. Usually, that person has more power. Sometimes that person is a friend. Friends can make this hard too.

I read parrhesia as a momentary act. Someone with less power says what they believe is true and accepts what follows.

What it is not

Venting releases pressure and can bring relief. Parrhesia aims at being heard by the person in front of you. Those are different aims.

Bluntness alone does not make speech parrhesia. Fast words can skip the harder question: are they also being said well?

Criticism from a person who holds power doesn't fit Foucault's account. He made this point carefully. A boss dressing down an employee has little at stake.

That speech isn't fearless. Power can make speaking easy. That moves the situation away from what Foucault described.

Oversharing has a different shape. Parrhesia is one true sentence to a particular person, with something real at stake.

What Foucault cared about most

Foucault linked parrhesia to caring for yourself. In the ancient world, telling the truth to a friend was considered a service. Friends were expected to speak plainly about your faults, and you were expected to take it. I read the practice as two people trying to help each other live better through honesty.

Foucault also connected parrhesia to how a person relates to themself. My reading is that speaking when it costs you can show what you actually believe. I don't mean that as a claim from Foucault.

For me, the payoff is a clearer sense of where you stand.

One objection is that this ancient account may not map neatly onto modern boundary-setting. Treating courage as a measure of good speech can leave people with less power carrying risks created by someone else's authority.

The honest caveat

Speaking up has costs, and people do not carry them equally. If your job, safety, visa, housing, or physical wellbeing depends on someone, that matters and should shape the decision. Nobody owes anyone fearless speech. Foucault described a rare, risky act, with no moral duty attached.

I find it more useful to name the true thing, count its cost, and choose deliberately. Sometimes silence is the choice. A person can read the room accurately and stay silent. Silence does not make them a coward.

What changes it from an outburst into a boundary

I understand a boundary as a sentence about your own actions. It says what you will do. It leaves the other person out of deciding who they must be.

These four examples show ways to put that into words.

At work, when a request keeps expanding
“I can take this on, but I need to drop one of the other two projects to do it well. Which one should come off my plate?”

It names the limit without accusing anyone, and gives the tradeoff to whoever created it. That's where honesty meets the boundary.

With a manager who moves the goalposts
“I want to hit the target you have in mind. Can we put the current version in writing so I am working against the same thing you are?”

It asks for a shared reference point without a confrontation. The written version can also protect the person asking for clarity.

With family, when a topic keeps coming back
“I love you and I am not going to talk about this at dinner. I will happily talk about anything else.”

The sentence stays short and warm. It does not turn the conversation into a case against the other person. It states your action without asking them to change their personality.

When someone asks you to explain a decision you have already made
“I have thought about it, and my answer is settled. I know you disagree, and I am okay with that.”

This can be the hardest example. It does not take on the task of making the other person comfortable with your choice. That is part of what makes the boundary clear.

All four follow the same pattern. Say what is true. Keep the sentence about your own action.

Over-explaining can invite negotiation. Discomfort may still be there. The examples leave room for it without rushing to fix it.

What I still don't know

How is parrhesia different from honest disagreement or a clear boundary? When is silence safer than speech?

The next time I rehearse a difficult sentence, I want to ask whose risk it carries and what would make speaking safer.

One thing to try this week

I could start with something I have rehearsed in my head for weeks. It needn't be the biggest issue or one that could put a job at risk. Small and real is enough.

Write it down first. Keep it under two lines. Make it about what you will do. Leave the other person's behavior out of the sentence.

Then say it once, at a normal volume, without following it with a paragraph of reasons.

Afterward, I want to check whether I still believe what I said. It is out of my head now. Parrhesia can give me that information.

item.title: The rules nobody said out loud
item.description: A student on the unspoken rules families run on: a quick test to find yours, why they made sense once, where I caught myself running mine, and three ways to spot your own.
item.content:encoded:
What does my family do when someone is upset?

Every family has a rulebook. Nobody wrote it down, and nobody remembers signing it. You just know it, the same way you know which stair creaks.

Here is a quick test. Finish this sentence the way your house would: “In our family, when someone is upset, we...”

Notice how fast the answer came. That speed is the rulebook.

Mine

In my house, love looked like food on the table and long work hours. My mom became a pharmacist, so a lot of her care showed up as effort. My dad was quiet and disciplined.

Nobody ever sat me down and said “we don’t talk about feelings here.” Feelings just got brushed off, and I learned the rule by watching what happened when someone brought one up.

I didn’t think of any of this as a pattern. It was just how families worked, as far as I knew. That’s the thing about unspoken rules. They feel like gravity.

Why they exist

I’ve stopped treating these rules as flaws. They usually made sense once. When a family is working hard to build a new life, there isn’t a lot of room for processing every feeling out loud. Work gets done.

Food gets made. Kids get through school. The rule “keep it together” kept people afloat.

My grandfather did construction work. I doubt anyone in that world had time to sit around naming emotions, and I don’t think they were wrong to prioritize getting through the day.

The trouble starts when the rule outlives the situation that created it. A rule that protected you at twenty can quietly limit you at forty.

In an article first published online on January 14, 2020, researchers studied 322 two-parent families with children ages 13 to 17. They found that facilitative family process rules were associated with more prosocial and less antisocial adolescent communication, while constraining rules were associated with more antisocial communication. The study was published in The Family Journal.

The findings leave room for another possibility: keeping some feelings private can protect privacy or stability in a particular setting. The study focused on two-parent families with adolescents, so it cannot represent every household or settle what a specific rule means.

Where I got it wrong

In training, a role-play client described a family almost identical to mine. My first instinct was to hand her the advice I wish I’d gotten. I had to stop and remind myself that her story isn’t mine, even when it sounds like it.

That was a lesson in how deep these rules run. I thought I was being helpful. I was actually running my own family’s rulebook on her.

Three ways to find your own

  • Watch what gets skipped. What topics does your family step around? Money, health, grief, anger? The gaps show you the rules.
  • Notice what gets praised. Being tough, being quiet, being the smart one, being no trouble. Praise teaches rules faster than lectures do.
  • Check your reflexes. When you’re stressed, what do you do first? Go silent, fix everything, joke, work harder? Odds are you learned that somewhere.

What to do with this

You don’t have to throw the rulebook out. Some of it is good. I’d keep the part about showing love through effort. I’m still deciding what to do about the part where feelings get brushed off.

Culture and family are the reason many of these rules exist, and they deserve respect. They can also be examined. Both can be true.

What I still don’t know

  • Which parts of this rulebook still express care in my family?

item.title: What therapy ethics codes get right and miss about culture
item.description: A student's read of the AAMFT and CAMFT codes of ethics through a multicultural lens: where they ask for respect and awareness, and where they stop short on power, privilege and systems.
item.content:encoded:
What should an ethics code ask a therapist to notice about culture and power? Every therapist I'll learn from follows a code of ethics. My program uses the AAMFT Code of Ethics (2015) and the CAMFT Code of Ethics (2020).

I read both through a multicultural lens for class. They do a lot right. I still have questions about what they leave out.

What the codes get right

Both ask therapists to respect clients and treat them fairly. AAMFT names diversity and inclusion as part of competent practice, prohibits discrimination, and calls for extra education or supervision when therapists work beyond their experience. Its social-responsibility language reaches beyond therapy.

CAMFT asks therapists to notice how their values and experiences shape their work, and treats continuing education and self-awareness as part of the job. Side by side, I saw both groups building cultural awareness into their rules.

Where I think they stop short

AAMFT talks about culture mostly through competence. That can make it sound like something a therapist masters and checks off. I don't think it works that way. I'm Vietnamese American, and my family still teaches me new things about my own culture.

The versions I read say little about power, privilege, or how unfair systems shape mental health and therapy. CAMFT mentions diversity, but I found its language broad and no direct discussion of intersectionality. That gap can make a "neutral" or color-blind stance easier, brushing past a client's lived experience.

I need to date that criticism. CAMFT's currently posted Code of Ethics says revised standards took effect December 6, 2025. My comments refer to the earlier CAMFT code I read for class. I should compare the current text before describing CAMFT's standards today.

Why it matters in practice

The codes set a solid floor of dignity and fairness. Beyond that, much depends on each therapist's judgment and self-awareness.

A code cannot spell out every context or family meaning. A detailed list might turn cultural humility into boxes to check, so there is a real reason to leave room for judgment. I can see that. I still wonder how clients can tell whether that judgment includes curiosity about power and history.

Reflection may help therapists who already examine their assumptions, but it may not reach someone who has not started. I hadn't thought about it this way until this assignment: a code relying on personal reflection can protect clients only as far as that reflection goes.

A bigger frame

Both codes seem shaped by a mostly Western, individual-focused way of thinking. They explain the expectation to respect differences, yet say less about the systems clients face before therapy. Culture also affects trust, communication, and what healing means. I'd like to see more of that spelled out.

What I still don't know

How do therapists and supervisors notice when culture shapes a clinical decision? What accountability is possible when a client and therapist read culture or power differently?

Where I'm going with this

I'm a student and may be missing parts of the picture. I want to keep asking where rules stop and my responsibility starts. That means reflecting on my own culture and assumptions, and asking clients about theirs without guessing.

I want to understand how supervision can keep that curiosity active when a code needs interpretation.

Check it yourself

Compare the AAMFT Code of Ethics with the currently posted CAMFT Code of Ethics. Check the version date before treating a class reading as current.

Sources: American Association for Marriage and Family Therapy. (2015). AAMFT code of ethics. California Association of Marriage and Family Therapists. (2020). CAMFT code of ethics.

item.title: Is there a perfect income? Why happiness seems to level off
item.description: A student reads the research on money and happiness: the famous $75,000 plateau, the studies that challenged it, and why more income matters less the more you have.
item.content:encoded:
For a long time I believed there was a number. If I earned enough, the stress would go away and I could finally relax. I think a lot of people my age carry a version of that number.

Growing up Asian American, money carried weight in my family. My grandfather did construction work, and my mom became a pharmacist. Every step up felt paid for by the generation before. When I started reading research on income and happiness, I wanted to know if the number was real.

Where the "$75,000" idea came from

In 2010, Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton analyzed more than 450,000 answers to a daily Gallup survey of Americans. They distinguished life evaluation, how people rate their lives overall, from emotional well-being, how their days feel, including joy, stress, sadness, or anger.

Life evaluation kept rising as income went up. Emotional well-being rose too, but past about $75,000 a year it stopped improving in their data. That finding became a headline people still repeat: money buys happiness up to $75,000, and then it stops.

The Census Bureau reported real median household income of $87,460 for 2025. Its release, published September 15, 2026, counts pretax money income and excludes in-kind transfers. That household statistic isn't a personal target, and it leaves room for differences in family size and cost of living. The Census Bureau's 2025 income release explains what the estimate measures.

The number moved

In 2018, Andrew Jebb's Purdue-led team used the Gallup World Poll, a sample of more than 1.7 million people. Their worldwide leveling points were about $95,000 for life evaluation and $60,000 to $75,000 for emotional well-being. Those amounts are for one person and likely higher for families. The point came later in wealthier regions; in some areas, people past it rated their lives a little lower.

That made me realize a "perfect income" depends a lot on where you live and what the people around you have.

Then someone found no plateau at all

In 2021, Matthew Killingsworth at Penn collected about 1.7 million in-the-moment check-ins from 33,391 working adults in the US, asking how they felt right then. Both kinds of happiness kept rising with income, with no plateau above $75,000.

Two careful studies disagreed. I liked that the researchers worked it out together: Kahneman and Killingsworth teamed with Barbara Mellers to reanalyze the data.

Both were right, for different people

Their 2023 paper found happiness kept climbing with income for most people. For the least happy 15 to 20 percent, it rose up to about $100,000, the old threshold adjusted for inflation, then mostly flattened. At the happiest end, it climbed faster above $100,000.

To me, money can fix problems that make life miserable: rent, debt, a car that keeps breaking down, or trouble seeing a doctor. Kahneman and Deaton also found low income makes divorce, illness, and being alone hurt more. Once those money problems are handled, what remains for that unhappy group may be grief, loneliness, or depression.

I want to be honest that this isn't settled. A fair counterargument is that observed patterns don't prove income caused well-being to change; in 2024, researchers questioned both the strength of the flattening and the causal story. I hold the $100,000 number loosely, though the broader pattern still seems consistent.

Why it levels off

Money works on a curve. In these studies, happiness tracks percentage change in income better than dollar change. Going from $30,000 to $60,000 doubles income; $200,000 to $230,000 adds the same dollars but only a 15 percent raise, which feels much smaller.

We get used to things. Psychologists call this hedonic adaptation. A raise or nicer apartment feels great for a while, then becomes normal. Jebb's team saw signs of adaptation and of wants growing with income.

We compare ourselves to the people around us. Erzo Luttmer found that, at the same personal income, people with higher-earning neighbors reported being less happy. This fits the higher leveling-off point in wealthier regions: when people around you earn more, "enough" goes up too.

Some of what shapes a good day has little to do with money. In Kahneman and Deaton's data, health, caregiving, loneliness, and smoking predicted daily emotions more strongly than income and education. Money can support those things, but can't stand in for them.

What this means for me

Looking back, the number I carried was mostly about safety. The research backs this up: getting out of real financial stress changes how life feels.

I'm trying to unlearn the idea that the number keeps growing. As someone training to be a therapist, I want to remember that money can carry meanings of security, worth, and family expectations. I'm still working on separating those for myself.

What I still don't know

How much of the connection between income and well-being reflects direct relief from financial stress, and how much reflects other parts of life that move alongside income? What does "enough" mean when housing, health care, and family responsibilities differ?

Over the next few years, I want to figure out what "enough" looks like for me, and then put more of my energy into time, health, and the people I care about.

Check it yourself

  • Kahneman and Deaton's 2010 study
  • The 2023 reanalysis
  • The 2024 critique
  • The Census Bureau's 2023 income report

Sources

  • Kahneman, D., & Deaton, A. (2010). High income improves evaluation of life but not emotional well-being. PNAS, 107(38), 16489-16493: the $75,000 emotional well-being plateau, the 450,000+ Gallup responses, and stronger daily-mood predictors like health and loneliness.
  • Jebb, A. T., Tay, L., Diener, E., & Oishi, S. (2018). Happiness, income satiation and turning points around the world. Nature Human Behaviour, 2, 33-38: the $95,000 and $60,000 to $75,000 global points and regional differences. Per-person note from Purdue's press release.
  • Killingsworth, M. A. (2021). Experienced well-being rises with income, even above $75,000 per year. PNAS, 118(4), e2016976118.
  • Killingsworth, M. A., Kahneman, D., & Mellers, B. (2023). Income and emotional well-being: A conflict resolved. PNAS, 120(10), e2208661120.
  • Rohrer, J. M., & Wenz, S. E. (2024). Inappropriate causal assumptions underlie Killingsworth, Kahneman, and Mellers' conclusions. PNAS, 121(46), e2313712121.
  • Arslan, R. C. (2024). The miseries that remain may yet be alleviated. PNAS, 121(46), e2314207121.
  • Luttmer, E. F. P. (2005). Neighbors as negatives: Relative earnings and well-being. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 120(3), 963-1002.

item.title: Love that showed up as food: growing up in a quiet Vietnamese American home
item.description: A student's story about a home where love came through cooking and fixing things instead of words, where that came from, and what I'm still working on as a future therapist.
item.content:encoded:
In my house, nobody said "I love you" very much. My mom cooked. My dad quietly fixed things around the house. If someone was upset, it usually got brushed off and dinner went on.

It took me a long time to see that as a pattern, and even longer to understand where it came from.

The house I grew up in

My parents have been married about twenty-five years. I grew up with them and my siblings under one roof. We were always together, though not always close emotionally.

My mom worked full time, cooked, cleaned, and carried most of the emotional weight at home. My dad was quiet and disciplined.

There was love. It showed up in actions. My mom's way of caring was food and acts of service, especially at family meals that pulled everybody to the same table. My siblings and I have always been close, and they've been my rocks through a lot.

Where it came from

My parents are both immigrants from Vietnam. They came from a culture that values discipline, humility, and hard work. Emotions can look like a distraction from getting through things, so they taught us to keep our heads down and not complain.

The Census Bureau counted 2,293,392 people in the Vietnamese-alone-or-in-any-combination group in 2020, in a release dated September 21, 2023. That racial category cannot describe how any household talks about feelings. The Census Bureau's data story explains the category.

That made me independent and guarded. Faith gave our home structure, community, and a real sense of service and forgiveness. It also brought pressure to appear composed, so emotions were managed quietly.

Food and acts of service can be real care while feelings stay unspoken. Context helps me understand my parents' habits, but it doesn't erase how the silence felt to me.

I don't blame my parents. Their way of caring made sense given what they had been through and what they were trying to give us.

What changed after I moved

I live in San Diego, far from Philadelphia. I feel more Americanized than I used to, but still pulled toward my Vietnamese roots. Away from home, Vietnamese food became a reminder of love and connection. My grandparents' stories and advice keep me grounded in what matters.

Christmas and Thanksgiving gatherings helped us connect in ways daily life didn't. Our family has also become more open over the years, and I'm grateful for that.

What I'm still working on

Knowing what it feels like to hold things in helps me connect with people who struggle to say what they feel. I'm still working on asking for help and trusting others with my emotions.

I used to see vulnerability as weakness. I don't anymore. I'd tell my younger self it's okay to speak up and he doesn't have to carry everything alone.

Why it matters to me as a future therapist

I want to work with immigrant families balancing culture, faith, and communication. My story is one version, and many Vietnamese American families look different, so I'll need to ask before I assume.

Try this yourself: think about how love was shown in your house when you were little. Who showed it, and how? Then ask whether that was the only way.

What I still don't know

What would my parents say they learned about showing love? How do I ask for help without feeling that I need to have all the words figured out first?

I'm still figuring out what healing looks like, and I want to keep practicing how to talk about what I need as I learn more about the family I came from.

item.title: Privilege is everything you never had to think about
item.description: A blunt student take on privilege: the list of things that were easy that you never noticed were easy, and how to start seeing your own.
item.content:encoded:
Let's get the fight out of the way. When people hear privilege, many hear "you're guilty" and stop listening. That's fair, given how the word gets thrown around. It also helps explain why the conversation goes nowhere.

My plain definition: privilege is the list of things that were easy for you that you never noticed were easy.

The invisible list

You don't feel privilege while you have it. Nobody wakes up thinking, "wow, I sure didn't get followed around the store today." The list becomes visible beside someone else's.

Some examples of things that can be on or off a person's list:

  • Walking into a room and not wondering if you're the only one like you
  • Never having to translate for your parents at the doctor's office
  • Having someone in your family who already went to college and could explain how it works
  • Having your name pronounced correctly on the first try
  • Not worrying that one bad day will be read as proof about your whole group

NCES reports that in 2021, home internet access through a computer was available to 98 percent of children ages 3 to 18 whose parents had a bachelor's degree or higher, compared with 78 percent whose parents had less than a high school credential. The indicator was updated in August 2023. This is a group comparison, not a full account of any child's life.

None of these make anyone bad. They're starting conditions. Some people get a tailwind, others a headwind, and many get both at different points.

Why this is not a scoreboard

I've seen this become a contest over who had it worse. I don't think that helps. Someone can be ahead in one area and behind in another. Social location is a stack, and it looks different for everybody.

The strongest objection is that privilege talk can rank people, discount effort, or sound like blame for hardship they didn't create. That risk is real when the idea replaces curiosity about someone's conditions.

I'm Vietnamese American. My family's story includes sacrifice I'm still figuring out how to repay. It brings real challenges.

My mom also worked hard enough to become a pharmacist, and my family valued school. Both are true; neither cancels the other.

What I got wrong

Early on, I assumed that if something was hard for me, it was hard for everyone like me. I treated my own list as the community's list. In training, I wanted to give a role-play client the advice I would have wanted. Her list wasn't mine.

That's the practical danger of not seeing your own privilege: you start giving advice that only works from your seat.

How to start seeing yours

Try this honestly. Nobody's checking:

  1. Write down three things that were easy in your life.
  2. Next to each one, write who helped make it easy.
  3. Write down one thing that was hard, and ask whether it was hard for everyone or just for people in your seat.

If step two gives you a long list of names, good. That's not shameful. That's information.

What I still don't know

How do I notice an advantage without assuming someone else's life is easier? What does accountability look like when I did not create a condition but may still benefit from it?

Where I'm going with this

I want to notice my list before someone else points it out and stop flinching when privilege comes up. The flinch is usually a signal worth looking at. Before I give advice, I want to ask what's easy for me that I've never had to think about, and whose help is underneath it.

Check it yourself

  • Peggy McIntosh's White Privilege Papers
  • U.S. Census Bureau: American Community Survey

item.title: One roll of toilet paper: what a week of scarcity taught me
item.description: A student's honest look at a class assignment where one roll had to last a week: how scarcity takes up headspace, why my frugality is a choice, and what it means for the clients I want to help.
item.content:encoded:
For one class assignment, I had to make a single roll of toilet paper last a whole week. That's it. No running to the store, no asking a roommate. One roll.

I thought it would be the easiest assignment of the semester. It became an annoying lesson in what scarcity does to your head.

Why it was easy for me, and why that's the point

I live in an apartment with my older brother, who has his own bathroom. I didn't share, so I controlled my use. I shop at Costco, where I can buy in bulk and stretch my money. One roll got me through the week without much trouble.

A mild inconvenience for me could be a real stressor for someone else.

What happened anyway

I started tracking the roll. I folded sheets more carefully, checked what remained, and calculated how long it would last.

Something I never think about became a small source of anxiety. I knew I could buy more once the assignment ended, but it took up more room in my head than I expected.

The part that felt like shame

The article we read, by Laszloffy and Habekost (2010), says this kind of task is meant to simulate daily life for people living in poverty. Scarcity isn't only having less. It brings stress, shame, and a constant need to keep track of what you have.

I never ran out. Imagining asking a classmate for a roll embarrassed me. I saw how vulnerable it can feel to admit you don't have enough, even over something small.

I used to think I was just frugal

I've always thought of myself as frugal. After this week, I realized that for me frugality is a choice: I can plan ahead, buy in bulk, and save because I have the money.

For many people, frugality isn't optional. Money problems pile onto everything else and drain energy that people with more cushion may not notice.

On September 15, 2026, the U.S. Census Bureau reported a 10.2% official poverty rate for 2025. Its measure uses pretax money income and excludes tax credits, so it offers one national measure, not a full account of household scarcity. The Census Bureau's 2025 income and poverty release explains the measure.

Why it matters for the work I want to do

I'm training to be a therapist. If one roll made me uncomfortable for a week, I can imagine how much harder it is to admit you can't provide food or shelter for your family.

Clients need a place to say those things without judgment. I want to respect their courage and resourcefulness. Scarcity can bring creativity, anxiety, irritability, or shame, and I shouldn't assume which I'm seeing.

A fair objection is that this week could not reproduce poverty: I knew it would end and could buy more. Treating temporary discomfort as understanding risks overstating what I learned.

What I still don't know

  • How might this land for someone who has lived with poverty?
  • What does one roll leave out about scarcity?
  • How can I listen without treating one uncomfortable week as knowledge of someone else's life?

Where I'm going with this

I want to keep checking my own privilege, because it's easy to forget when things are comfortable. Next time I hear someone called "bad with money," I want to ask what they were working with first.

Source: Laszloffy, T. A., & Habekost, J. (2010). Using experiential tasks to enhance cultural sensitivity among MFT trainees. Journal of Marital and Family Therapy, 36(3), 333-346. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1752-0606.2010.00213.x

item.title: The "I Am" poem and who we say we are
item.description: A student on writing an "I Am" poem for a capstone class: where people start, why heritage lines carry so much, and why reading it out loud was the hard part.
item.content:encoded:
What do I choose to put after “I am”?

What it is

An “I Am” poem is a simple template. Every line starts with the same two words, “I am,” and you finish the sentence. Some versions also use “I wonder,” “I hear,” “I want,” and “I hope.” The structure is small, so there’s nowhere to hide.

I wrote mine for my capstone class, as part of my minor in Counseling and Social Change. We were asked to write it, share it with the class, and talk about it afterward. Writing it was easy. Reading it out loud in front of the whole class was the hard part.

Where people start

A lot of people start with identity, and a lot of those lines are about heritage. A few examples of what someone might write:

  • I am Vietnamese American.
  • I am Italian American.
  • I am Hispanic.
  • I am a mutt.

They look similar on paper, but each one carries a different story. “I am Vietnamese American” can hold a whole family history of migration. “I am a mutt” is usually said with a laugh, and it tells you the person has a mix of backgrounds and doesn’t have one tidy label for it.

In an August 12, 2021 report on the 2020 Census, the U.S. Census Bureau counted 33.8 million people who identified with two or more races. The Bureau also cautioned that comparisons with 2010 need care because the race questions, processing, and coding changed. Read the Census Bureau’s report and its caveat.

The part I noticed

Labels like these are the ones we’ve been handed by forms, census boxes, and the questions people ask when they meet us. Writing “I am” and finishing it yourself is different, because you choose which label goes first and whether it fits at all.

At the same time, a self-chosen line cannot control how other people or institutions label us. A short poem may be too small for an identity that keeps changing.

Culture matters here. My Vietnamese American background grounds me the most and gives me the most direction. Being Christian is part of my answer too, and that’s something I’m still grappling with.

Some people lead with their heritage. Others skip it and write about what they do or who they love. Both are real answers.

Why I keep writing these

I took a class on finding your identity, and I write things like this because I hope my answers stay true over time and that the writing helps. Some of it is still unfinished, and I’m okay with that.

Try it yourself

Give yourself ten minutes and start every line with “I am.” Don’t edit while you write. Then read it back and see which line you almost left out.

You don’t have to share it. I shared mine in class, but I’m keeping it off the blog for now.

What I still don’t know

  • Will the lines I choose still feel true next year?
  • What might I leave out when I only have ten minutes?
  • How much do other people’s questions shape which line I put first?

I’m a student sharing what I’m learning. This isn’t therapy or clinical advice.

Next, I want to write another one in a year and see which lines have changed.

  • The Census Bureau’s 2020 Census data tables, including the redistricting supplementary tables.
  • Connecticut Department of Children and Families’ “Who I Am” poem exercise.

item.title: Social privilege: we didn't all start at the same line
item.description: A student's honest take on social privilege: a privilege-walk video, the statement that caught me off guard, why effort isn't the whole story, and a short exercise to find your own line.
item.content:encoded:
Last fall, one of my classes had us watch a video called What Is Privilege? A group of people stood side by side in one straight line. Someone read statements out loud, and people stepped forward or back when each one was true for them.

Everyone started even. By the end, they were spread out all over the place. Nobody in that line had picked where they ended up. They were answering questions about lives they were born into.

The statement that got me

Most statements were ones I expected, about money, race, and safety. Then one came up about growing up with both parents in the home. I had never thought of that as privilege.

It was just my normal. Two parents can mean more stability, more support, more hands, and more money. That foundation can shape a child's life, and almost nobody counts it when they talk about who "earned" what.

That doesn't mean a home with one parent is missing love. Plenty of single parents hold everything together and raise kids who feel deeply cared for. The privilege is in the extra time and resources, not in how much a family loves each other.

That was the moment privilege stopped feeling like a word other people needed to think about.

In its September 2025 report, the Census Bureau lists 2024 official poverty rates of 4.3% for married-couple families and 21.8% for families with a female householder and no spouse present. These family-level rates do not explain the difference or measure an individual child's support. See Table A-2.

Where I'd be standing

Watching people move forward and backward made me uncomfortable. Knowing inequality exists is one thing. Seeing it laid out among real people made it hard to look away from.

So I tried to figure out where I'd be standing. I'm Vietnamese American. I've had real advantages, like access to education. I've also dealt with cultural stereotypes and felt out of place in rooms where nobody looked like me.

I'd probably be somewhere in the middle, stepping forward on some questions and back on others. Privilege comes in layers. Most people have some of it and lack some of it, and which layer matters depends on the room you're in.

The effort story

Here's the blunt part. A lot of people believe success only comes down to effort. Work hard and you'll make it. If you didn't make it, you didn't work hard enough.

Effort matters. I believe that. The strongest counterargument is that effort and choices shape outcomes, and people can change their starting conditions. A line exercise cannot measure anyone's effort or predict their future.

But that story skips over the starting line, and that's where prejudice sneaks in. Once you believe everyone started even, the people behind you start to look lazy. You end up blaming them for barriers they never built and can't always see past.

Why this matters to me

I'm training to be a therapist, and clients will come from every kind of background. Without thinking about privilege, I could miss big parts of their story.

If a client struggles and my answer is basically "just work harder," without noticing the systems pushing against them, I could do real harm. I'd be asking them to fit my standard when my job is to meet them where they are.

The same goes outside therapy. It's easy to assume everyone has the same chances as you. I need to ask what someone might be up against.

It's not about guilt

The video also reminded me of something I needed to hear. Privilege isn't about feeling guilty. I didn't choose the circumstances I was born into, and neither did you.

What I do get to choose is how I respond. I can use the advantages I have to understand other people better, question my own assumptions, and show some empathy before I judge.

Try your own line

Grab a piece of paper. For each statement that's true for you, make a tally mark. Nobody is grading this, and there's no good or bad score.

  1. I grew up with both parents in the home.
  2. My family never worried about keeping the lights on.
  3. The language spoken at home matched the language at school.
  4. I saw people who looked like me in my textbooks and on TV.
  5. My family could help me pay for college.
  6. I've never been followed around a store.
  7. I've never had to wonder if a building would be accessible to me.

Now count your marks. Whatever your number is, it says something about where you started, not about what you're worth. If your count was high, it might be worth thinking about how different the same questions would feel for someone with a lower one.

What I still don't know

What fits inside a yes-or-no answer like “I grew up with both parents”? How can I ask about someone's starting point without treating it as their whole story?

Where I'm going with this

I want to keep building this awareness, because it's easy to lose. Next time I catch myself thinking someone just needs to try harder, I want to ask what their line looked like first.

item.title: Social location: where you stand decides what you see
item.description: A blunt student take on social location: the stack of race, class, family and culture that decides what you notice, what you miss, and what you call normal.
item.content:encoded:
You were not born looking at the world from nowhere. Where you stand changes what you see, miss, and assume is "normal."

That spot has a name in my field: social location.

What it actually is

Social location is your mix of race, class, gender, age, religion, language, ability, immigration story, and where you grew up. No one has only one. The parts stack, shaping how people treat you, what doors open, and what you never had to think about.

Think of stadium seats: the front row sees sweat; behind a pole, half the field. Both people may say "I watched the whole game." Only one is right, usually not the person in the good seat.

My seat

I'm Vietnamese American. My grandfather did construction work; my mom became a pharmacist. In my house, love looked like food on the table and long work hours, and feelings were usually brushed off instead of talked about.

During training, a role-play client described almost the same family. I wanted to give her the advice I wish somebody had given me, then stopped myself. Her story isn't mine. My seat is not her seat, even when the view looks close.

That was when social location stopped being a vocabulary word for me.

The part people skip

Everyone loves the idea until it points at them. Talking about others' seats is easy; looking at your own is where people get quiet.

So, plainly:

  • If something has always been easy for you, check why before you call it talent.
  • If something has always been hard for you, check why before you call it your fault.
  • If you've never had to explain a part of yourself to a room, that is information about your seat, not about the room.

None of this means one group is good and another is bad. You and I have different data, and pretending we don't is how people talk past each other for years.

NCES reports that in 2021, computer-based home internet access was available to 98 percent of children ages 3 to 18 in families in the highest income quarter, compared with 85 percent in the lowest. The indicator was updated in August 2023 using American Community Survey data. This is a group estimate, not an explanation of every family's situation.

The strongest caution is that categories can become shortcuts: group patterns do not tell me an individual's story, and overlapping identities can be flattened when the framework is applied mechanically.

Why it matters for helping people

I'm training to be a therapist, so I care about this. If I treat every client like a copy of me, I'll miss most of what they tell me. A behavior can look like a problem from my seat and look like survival from theirs. Culture is usually the reason, and I can't see the reason if I never ask.

Sharing a label doesn't mean I understand a client. Two Asian American people can come from totally different homes. In training, we leaned toward shared assumptions fast, and some were wrong.

A quick exercise

Grab a piece of paper and answer these. No one is grading it.

  1. Where did I grow up, and who else lived there?
  2. What did my family teach me about money, school, and feelings?
  3. What do I get treated as "default" in? What do I get treated as "different" in?
  4. Who would see my life very differently, and why?

Question four is the hard one. Sit with it longer than feels comfortable.

What I still don't know

Which parts of a person's context are useful to ask about, and which am I assuming too quickly? How can I keep a pattern in mind while letting the person's own account lead?

Where I'm going with this

I want to ask before assuming. I'm still working on it and will probably mess it up again. I'd rather catch myself in the mirror than have a client catch me in the room.

I want to notice when I say "that's just how things are," try adding "from where I'm standing," and ask what I still need to learn.

Check it yourself

  • NCES: Children's Internet Access at Home
  • U.S. Census Bureau: American Community Survey
  • Kimberlé Crenshaw, “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex”

Student writing, not clinical advice. If you are struggling, a licensed professional or a local crisis line can help.

item.title: What a Freudian slip can and cannot tell us
item.description: A student's look at Freud, slips of the tongue, and the unconscious: what Freud claimed, what researchers found since, and where schemas and attachment theory fit.
item.content:encoded:
A note before we begin: I am a student sharing what I am learning. This is not therapy and it does not diagnose or treat anything.

What can a word that came out wrong really tell us?

A Freudian slip usually tells you less than people think. I first heard about it as a word that comes out before I plan it, maybe from a part of the mind I can't see. I've had that happen.

I said something that didn't match what I meant, and it didn't feel like a statement about who I am. So I went and read what Freud claimed and what research says now.

What Freud said

In 1901, Freud wrote The Psychopathology of Everyday Life. Freud called slips faulty actions, claiming they let repressed unconscious wishes leak out. Linguist Mark Liberman collected examples on the blog Language Log.

The president of the Austrian Parliament announced, “I take notice that a full quorum of members is present and herewith declare the sitting closed!” A member of the House of Commons named the honourable member for “Central Hell” instead of Hull. A woman tried to compliment her friend's hat and said, “I am sure you must have thrown this delightful hat together,” when she meant sewn.

Funny examples. Freud's theory changed over time. His earlier model split the mind into conscious, preconscious, and unconscious; his later one used the id, ego, and superego, while both models stayed in his thinking. The id seeks satisfaction now, the ego deals with reality, and the superego is the internalized voice of parents and society.

What researchers found later

Language Log notes that people make about one slip for every thousand words they speak. Speaking is a hard job for the brain, and many slips look like errors made while it builds a sentence. Psychologist Michael Motley tested this. With fake electrodes and the threat of a mild shock, people's slips leaned toward electrical words.

In a sexual context, the slips leaned that way. So what's on your mind can tip a slip. The same experiment showed that slips are easy to produce for plain sound reasons.

Mick Power summarized later research for the British Psychological Society in 2000. Modern research supports much behavior running automatically outside awareness, but not Freud's instinctual energy base. It also questions how much unconscious activity comes from repression. Freud relied mainly on therapy sessions, which are hard to test from outside.

A fair counterargument is that context can shape slips: in a 1979 experiment, Motley and Baars found more electricity-related slips in a shock-focused context and more sex-related slips in a sex-focused one. This supports a context effect, though it cannot show what an individual slip means. Their study abstract.

What stays with us from early life

People develop ideas about themselves and the world that can stick. Psychologists call these schemas. The American Psychological Association defines a schema as a collection of basic knowledge guiding perception and interpretation; it notes that negative schemas, such as “I am a damaged person,” can come from early childhood experiences.

Attachment theory is related but separate. John Bowlby developed it, and Mary Ainsworth expanded it. It describes how infant-caregiver relationships shape later emotional development.

Bowlby's internal working model is an APA-defined mental picture of the self, other people, and relationships, formed through early caregiving. That looks like the closest link to what I grew up with. I haven't read enough yet to say more than that.

What I still don't know

  • How can we tell a passing context from a more persistent concern?

I want to notice context before drawing conclusions from a slip.

What I want to try

Next time a word comes out wrong, I want to check the boring explanations first. Was I tired? Was I rushing?

The reading makes me think those cover most slips. I'll keep paying attention and see what I notice.

Check it yourself

  • Freud, Psychopathology of Everyday Life (English, 1914).
  • Motley and Baars's 1979 study, PubMed.

Sources

  • Language Log, Mark Liberman, “Freudian slip of the week” (a linguist's lecture notes, not a study): Freud's 1901 book, his examples of slips, the rate of about one slip per thousand words, and Motley's 1980 experiment.
  • Mick Power, British Psychological Society, “Freud and the unconscious” (18 December 2000): how Freud's models changed, and which parts modern research supports.
  • Encyclopædia Britannica, “Sigmund Freud: Psychoanalytic theory”: the conscious, preconscious, and unconscious model, and the id, ego, and superego.
  • Freud Museum London, “What is Psychoanalysis? The Ego, the Id and the Superego”: what each part does.
  • APA Dictionary of Psychology, “schema”.
  • APA Dictionary of Psychology, “internal working model”.
  • Mechanisms and fundamental principles in Freudian psychoanalysis (Taylor & Francis, 2023): Freud kept the topographical model alongside the structural one.
  • APA Dictionary of Psychology, “attachment theory”.

item.title: What Arendt meant by the banality of evil
item.description: Hannah Arendt watched Adolf Eichmann's trial and coined a phrase people still misread. What she claimed, what critics say, and why thinking matters.
item.content:encoded:
What did Hannah Arendt mean when she called evil banal?

The phrase is often flattened into a lazy excuse for stopping thought. In spring 1961, Adolf Eichmann sat in a glass booth in a Jerusalem courtroom, answering questions about the deaths of millions. He had run Nazi deportation logistics.

Israeli agents captured him in Argentina the year before, and he stood trial for crimes against the Jewish people. Philosopher Hannah Arendt watched and reported on the trial for The New Yorker. The phrase “banality of evil” has been quoted, misquoted, and argued over ever since.

What she saw in the courtroom

Many expected a monster, which can make her point easy to miss. Arendt described a man who could barely speak without falling back on stock phrases and clichés. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy summarizes her view this way: she saw a “clown” where many expected a “monster,” and linked his deeds in part to “thoughtlessness.” She meant an inability to look at anything from another person's point of view.

The book that followed, Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil, carried the phrase in its subtitle and used it once more near the end. Arendt explained the point later in a letter to the scholar Gershom Scholem. Evil, she wrote, is never “radical.” It is only extreme, and it can lay waste to the world because it spreads “like a fungus on the surface.”

What the phrase does not say

Some people hear the phrase as meaning evil is boring or Eichmann was a harmless clerk who followed orders. Arendt's account says he pursued the deportations with zeal; she supported his death sentence and held him fully responsible for what he did.

The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum reports that Eichmann and his aides deported some 440,000 Hungarian Jews from late April to early July 1944. The Museum's account records the estimate and dates.

The phrase describes Eichmann's character and motives as he appeared to Arendt in court. The Stanford Encyclopedia notes she did not mean it as a general theory of Nazi evil.

The argument that followed

Criticism began right away, and some of it has held up. The strongest objection, made by historian Bettina Stangneth in Eichmann Before Jerusalem and others, is that Arendt mistook Eichmann's courtroom performance for his character, underweighted his antisemitism, and left his deliberate choices underexplained. Her book also drew anger for its tone and claims about the Jewish Councils, bodies the Nazis forced Jewish communities to form. The Stanford Encyclopedia outlines this criticism.

I think both things can be true at once. The trial may have shown Arendt a face that was partly staged. Her larger question stays with me: how do ordinary people take part in terrible things without feeling that they have decided anything?

Thinking as a habit

Arendt kept working on that question. She asked whether “the habit of examining whatever happens to come to pass” might help people refrain from evil. For her, thinking was a silent dialogue with oneself.

In her essay on personal responsibility under dictatorship, she described the few people who refused to collaborate. They did not have firmer moral rules than their neighbors. They asked whether they could still live in peace with themselves after doing a certain deed. “I cannot walk away from myself,” she wrote.

That seems like a modest standard to me. It does not require heroism or a philosophy degree. It asks for a pause long enough to consider what an action is and who it lands on.

Why it still gets quoted

Arendt wrote about totalitarian rule, so comparisons need care. Most workplace shortcuts and bureaucratic habits are nowhere near the Final Solution. I can still see her observation carrying over in a small way to ordinary life. People repeat the phrases of their institution, follow the form, and tell themselves someone else owns the decision.

That kind of noticing takes practice. It can start with small things: a policy someone repeats without having read, or a line passed along because everyone else does. I want to catch the moment when a phrase starts doing the thinking for me.

What I still don't know

  • How much can courtroom behavior show about motive?
  • How can the phrase travel without flattening the history it came from?

I want to check Arendt's account and the trial record before carrying the phrase elsewhere.

Check it yourself

  • Arendt's original New Yorker report.
  • USHMM trial footage, July 3, 1961.
  • Stanford Encyclopedia, sections 6.1 to 6.3.

Further reading

  • Hannah Arendt, Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil (1963)
  • Hannah Arendt, “Personal Responsibility under Dictatorship” and “Thinking and Moral Considerations”
  • Bettina Stangneth, Eichmann Before Jerusalem: The Unexamined Life of a Mass Murderer (2014)

Sources

  • Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Hannah Arendt”, sections 6.1 to 6.3: the “clown” and “thoughtlessness” language, the letter to Scholem, the critics including Stangneth, the death sentence, and the quotations on thinking and conscience.
  • United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, “Adolf Eichmann”: his role in the deportations, capture in Argentina in 1960, the 1961 trial in Jerusalem, the December 1961 verdict, and the 1962 execution.

item.title: Philadelphia protests and rallies, late October to early November

item.content:encoded:

Peaceful assembly is a protected right, and showing up is one of the oldest ways people take part in public life.
