item.title: What we teach men about pain: stigma, silence, and the help that misses them
item.description: Why help so often fails to reach men: what the CDC and NIMH numbers show, what may be missed, and the rules many of us inherit.
item.content:encoded:
A note before we begin: I am doing well. I am writing this piece to draw attention to a problem I see around me, and I am not writing it from a crisis of my own.

What does it cost when boys learn to keep pain to themselves?

We teach men to hide pain, then wonder why they stay quiet. Males are about half the U.S. population and nearly 80 percent of its suicide deaths, according to the CDC (2023 figures). In 2024 the male suicide rate was nearly four times the female rate. I am training to become a marriage and family therapist; those numbers have stayed with me since I first read them.

I grew up as an Asian American boy in a house where hard feelings stayed quiet and private. Nobody announced the rule. Adults passed along what they had been taught, and I absorbed it.

Years later, I keep asking what the silence costs and why professional help misses men. This essay asks without blaming men or women.

What the numbers show

Suicide is the most severe outcome in a wider pattern. The CDC reports this sex disparity each year; a federal brief shows the male rate was three to four times the female rate throughout 2014 to 2024.

The National Center for Health Statistics' September 2026 report gives a more concrete view: the 2024 age-adjusted male rate was 22.3 deaths per 100,000 standard population. The report and its tables use final mortality data.

In the National Institute of Mental Health's summary of 2022 survey data, 41.6 percent of men with any mental illness received past-year treatment, compared with 56.9 percent of women. For adults with serious mental illness, the figures were 59.3 percent of men and 71.4 percent of women.

Women are diagnosed with depression and anxiety more often, so their higher treatment rate does not mean they are doing well. The figures suggest care reaches a smaller share of men who need it. The survey was conducted in English and recorded only male and female categories, so it cannot describe every population.

These comparisons cannot explain why treatment use or suicide rates differ. Underlying distress, recognition, reporting, resources, and access may also matter. A men-focused essay can miss the needs of women and people outside the survey's male and female categories. I can take the disparity seriously while staying careful about its causes.

Distress that goes unrecognized

Part of the gap may reflect what clinicians and screening tools notice. In a 2013 JAMA Psychiatry study, Martin and colleagues found depressed men reported more anger attacks, substance use, and risk-taking than depressed women. Standard checklists omit these symptoms.

Adding them to the usual symptoms erased the difference in depression rates in their sample. A checklist that misses them is a lousy gatekeeper.

One study cannot settle the question. Distress may go unrecognized in some men. Someone whose depression appears as irritability or heavy drinking can pass a standard screen unidentified.

The rules many men inherit

The American Psychological Association's guidelines for work with boys and men note that traits associated with masculinity, such as courage and leadership, are often linked to good health. Other masculine norms can cause harm. Men taught to suppress emotion are less willing to seek help.

Wong, Ho, Wang, and Miller (2017) pooled 78 samples with more than 19,000 participants. Conformity to masculine norms was modestly associated with poorer mental health and moderately associated with less help-seeking. Self-reliance was among the norms most consistently tied to poor outcomes.

Primacy of work showed no significant relationship to any outcome. These are correlations and cannot establish cause.

That result complicates a lazy story about work. Responsibility and providing for others may carry little risk on their own. Managing everything alone appears more closely tied to harm.

One perspective among many

I can speak only for myself. Research on Asian Americans finds lower mental health service use than in the general population, and higher use among U.S.-born Asian Americans than immigrants (Abe-Kim et al., 2007). Family expectations, immigration history, and generation all appear to play a part. Asian American men are a large and varied group, and my experience is one account among many.

Family systems theory helps me see how “handle it quietly” can travel through generations without a villain. Each person may be responding sensibly to the circumstances they faced.

What may help

I do not have one remedy. A few approaches have support or plausible logic. Help may land more readily when framed through values men already hold, such as building strength, solving a problem, or caring for people who depend on them.

Families, friends, and workplaces can make it routine to ask a second question after “How are you?” Clinicians can ask about anger, sleep, drinking, and risk-taking along with sadness.

What I still don't know

Whether a practical first conversation would bring more men through the door remains an open question. The answer probably varies from person to person.

How can clinicians ask about anger, sleep, drinking, or risk-taking without deciding too quickly what those signs mean for a particular person? Which approaches help men feel able to seek support while honoring differences in family, culture, and identity?

I want to keep thinking about how that first question is asked.

If you or someone you know is struggling

In the United States, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at any hour. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911. This essay is a personal reflection and does not offer medical advice or treatment.

Check it yourself

  • CDC/NCHS, Changes in Suicide Rates in the United States From 2023 to 2024 (final 2024 mortality data).
  • NIMH, Mental Illness (2022 NSDUH treatment figures).
  • Martin and colleagues' 2013 JAMA Psychiatry study (the original article).
  • American Psychological Association, Guidelines for Psychological Practice with Boys and Men (2018 PDF).

Sources

  • CDC, Suicide Data and Statistics (2024 rates by sex). The 2023 figure of 50 percent of the population and nearly 80 percent of suicides comes from an earlier version of the same CDC page.
  • NIMH, Mental Illness statistics (2022 NSDUH data, treatment by sex).
  • Martin, L. A., Neighbors, H. W., & Griffith, D. M. (2013). The experience of symptoms of depression in men vs women. JAMA Psychiatry, 70(10), 1100–1106.
  • Wong, Y. J., Ho, M.-H. R., Wang, S.-Y., & Miller, I. S. K. (2017). Meta-analyses of the relationship between conformity to masculine norms and mental health-related outcomes. Journal of Counseling Psychology, 64(1), 80–93.
  • American Psychological Association (2018). Guidelines for Psychological Practice with Boys and Men.
  • Abe-Kim, J., et al. (2007). Use of mental health-related services among immigrant and US-born Asian Americans. American Journal of Public Health, 97(1), 91–98.
  • Garnett, M. F., & Zehner, A. M. (2026, September). Changes in Suicide Rates in the United States From 2023 to 2024 (NCHS Data Brief No. 572). (2024 age-adjusted rates by sex).

item.title: When a label becomes the problem: power/knowledge meets diagnosis
item.description: Foucault on power, knowledge and norms: labels can help people, and it is still fair to ask who decided where the line goes.
item.content:encoded:
Labels make messy lives look neat. Forms offer boxes: good, fair, poor. Normal, elevated, high.

The lines look settled. Someone picked where each one belongs.

Foucault's early work on madness

Foucault's first major book, History of Madness (1961), follows a category across centuries. In the Renaissance, madness could have a strange, unsettling voice, sometimes treated as insight. During the great confinement in the 1600s, people called mad were locked away with the poor and idle. Later, medicine made madness a condition to study, diagnose, and treat.

Foucault did not claim that nothing was ever wrong with anyone. He argued that “madness” was no fixed object waiting to be discovered. Institutions redrew the category, shaping who got heard, locked up, and given authority to set the terms.

The medical gaze

In The Birth of the Clinic (1963), Foucault describes medicine's changing view of people. The patient's story can fade; the patient can become a case, a body to read, and a set of signs to classify. He called this way of seeing the medical gaze.

That gaze has a purpose. It helps doctors learn to see patterns quickly enough to help. It remains one way of looking.

Every way of looking has blind spots. I keep thinking about what gets missed when someone falls outside the pattern.

Discipline and the norm

Discipline and Punish (1975) brings the discussion closer to ordinary life. I covered the panopticon earlier. Norms are the other half of that book.

Foucault argued modern institutions punish what is wrong and produce standards for what counts as normal, then measure people against them. Schools rank, clinics classify, workplaces evaluate. Familiar measurements can look like plain descriptions of reality while the choices behind them fade from view.

I see that as a bridge between the norm and the label.

Power/knowledge

This ties earlier themes together: Foucault connected knowledge and power, arguing they are produced together. Whoever can name something shapes how it is seen, studied, and treated.

A diagnosis carries knowledge and can involve power. Credentials give someone authority to name what another person is living through.

The part people get wrong

People often read Foucault as saying medicine is a lie or diagnosis is oppression. That misses his argument. To me, it does little to help anyone understand it.

Diagnoses can be lifesaving. They can open doors to care, insurance, accommodations, and community. A diagnosis can give someone a word for something they carried alone for years. Naming a pattern can bring relief.

His point is more specific. People make labels in history and for particular reasons. We can ask what a label does and whether it is accurate.

Shared categories matter too. On 25 May 2019, WHO reported Member States agreed to adopt ICD-11, effective 1 January 2022. WHO calls the ICD the international standard for reporting diseases and health conditions, and says it supports clinical records, research, patient safety, reimbursement, and health-resource decisions. Common categories make patterns comparable and help plan services, while each code still describes only part of a person. WHO's 25 May 2019 World Health Assembly update.

When the label becomes the self

The risk can be hard to notice. Once a category exists, it can take up too much space around the person it describes.

A diagnosis describes one part of a person. When every appointment, form, and conversation runs through the label, it can become easy to tell your whole life in its language. Foucault worried that sorting happens so smoothly people may stop noticing it, whether or not they were sorted correctly.

Norms also sort people into normal and not. Being placed on the wrong side of that line can affect how others treat you. That weight comes from the social world around a person. It deserves its own name.

So what do you do with this

Keep the care. Question how the label is being used.

When a label lands, I think this question is worth asking: “who decided this is where the line goes, what was that decision built on, and what does the label do to how I see myself?” A diagnosis can be useful. Keep some distance from it.

Notice what the category leaves out. A category is like a map. Maps leave out most of the territory.

What I still don't know

Which parts of a diagnosis feel accurate to the person who receives it? How can a clinician leave room for that person's account when a form asks for one category? What would make it easy to revisit a label after circumstances change?

One thing to try this week

Choose one label you carry, a diagnosis, type, personality result, or something in your file. Write two lists. First, what the label has given you: access, words, treatment, understanding, community. Second, what it has never described: parts that do not fit, days it does not explain, and things you would still be if it vanished tomorrow.

Then read the second list again. I want to keep asking what else belongs in a story when a label starts to feel like the whole thing.

Check it yourself

  • WHO's 2019 ICD-11 announcement, its adoption and uses.
  • WHO's ICD-11 browser, to explore the classification.
  • Foucault's “Panopticism”, the original text.

Further reading

  • Michel Foucault, History of Madness (1961)
  • Michel Foucault, The Birth of the Clinic (1963)
  • Michel Foucault, Discipline and Punish (1975), the section on normalization
  • Michel Foucault, Power/Knowledge (1980), collected interviews and essays

Talk with a clinician you trust about your own care, and in the US call or text 988 if you are in crisis.

Sources

  • Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Michel Foucault”, his work on madness, the clinic, and normalization.
  • Foucault, Discipline and Punish, “Panopticism” (foucault.info), how observation and judgment shape people.

item.title: The watcher in your pocket: the panopticon meets social media
item.description: How a prison design from 1786 explains why we edit ourselves online, and one small thing to try this week.
item.content:encoded:
What does my phone have to do with Jeremy Bentham's Panopticon? I think it can feel like a pocket-sized panopticon, with serious limits.

In 1786, English philosopher Jeremy Bentham visited his brother Samuel in Russia. The basic idea came from Samuel. Jeremy sketched a prison called the Panopticon.

Cells formed a ring around a central tower. Each cell was lit and open to the tower. One guard could look into any cell at any moment. Prisoners could never tell when they were being watched.

That is the design's sharp trick, and its cruelty. The guard did not have to be there. People who believed they might be seen began policing themselves. Bentham called it a “new mode of obtaining power of mind over mind.”

Foucault's point

Almost two hundred years later, Michel Foucault took up the design in Discipline and Punish (1975), using it to make a larger argument about power. He argued that modern power often works through discipline, not only violence or public spectacle. Schools, barracks, hospitals, factories, and prisons share tools: timetables, exams, ranks, files, and constant visibility.

The Panopticon became a symbol for that argument. You cannot tell when the eye is on you, so you act as if it is always there. Foucault described the inmate this way: “is seen, but he does not see; he is the object of information, never a subject in communication.”

Power moves from something done to you into something you do to yourself. People learn to manage their behavior in advance, without anyone having to break them. Foucault called the result a docile body.

He also wrote about norms that sort people as normal and abnormal, healthy and unhealthy, employable and not. Those categories can feel like facts, even when they come from an institution's decision about what to measure.

So what does this have to do with your phone

A social-media feed reminds me of the Panopticon. You are not in a cell, and there is no tower. The comparison can still be useful.

Your profile is like the cell: lit, legible, and there to be seen. Your audience takes the place of the tower. You cannot see who is looking or when. A post's number offers a rough proxy for attention, though it never tells you who the eye belongs to.

Algorithms do more than watch. They rank and predict. Instagram's May 31, 2023 explanation says different parts of the app use separate ranking systems, and Feed ranking draws on thousands of signals.

That is the company's account, not an outside audit. Instagram's explanation of how ranking works describes how posts are surfaced. These systems decide whose post travels and whose disappears, which connects to Foucault's point about what gets noticed.

Then comes the part Foucault might recognize most: you start doing the work for them.

You might draft a caption three times, check the post again at 11pm, or leave out a strange or unfinished thought because it will not perform. Nobody forced those choices. You made them after taking in the possibility of being watched.

That is the loop: self-censorship from within, with no censor above.

Two honest caveats

The strongest counterargument is that ranking can make a huge feed useful, and many posts reach friends and followers who chose to connect. Instagram points to Following and Favorites as controls. Those choices matter, though they do not explain every post's reach.

The comparison has limits. Bentham's guard had authority; your audience mostly does not. Likes carry no prison sentence.

Foucault wrote about institutions with power to confine, classify, and treat people. Use the image as a comparison, not a diagnosis of your feed.

Foucault did not offer five steps to a happier life. He wrote about how power circulates and how people push back. In his framing, critique is the art of not being governed quite so much.

That last idea feels useful here. You cannot log out of power. I want to keep in view where the gaze has moved from the tower into my own head. Then I can decide how much of my life it gets to author.

What I still don't know

How much of my self-editing is for people I know, and how much for a ranking system? What can a platform's public explanation tell me about why a post appeared?

I want to notice when I am writing to someone and when I am writing for the number beside the post.

One thing to try this week

Choose one thing you would have posted and leave it unposted. Say it to a friend, write it in a notebook, or leave it in your head. This is a small experiment, not a punishment or a decision to quit social media.

Notice how much attention goes into anticipating the reaction. See what happens to the sentence when nobody is grading it.

If that feels too small, try the reverse. Post something deliberately unoptimized. No hook, no hashtags, no timing strategy. See if the sky falls.

As you scroll, ask one more question: who is measuring what? Every feed makes judgments about what deserves to be seen. You are allowed to have opinions about the judge.

Check it yourself

  • Read Foucault's primary text, “Panopticism.”
  • Read Instagram's May 31, 2023 ranking explanation.
  • See the UCL Bentham Project history.

Further reading

  • Michel Foucault, Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison (1975), the panopticism section
  • Jeremy Bentham, Panopticon, or the Inspection House (1791)
  • Michel Foucault, “What Is Critique?” (1978 lecture)
  • Shoshana Zuboff, The Age of Surveillance Capitalism (2019), the commercial version of the gaze

Sources

  • Foucault, Discipline and Punish, “Panopticism” (foucault.info), the Panopticon, and the line “He is seen, but he does not see.”
  • University of Chicago Press, “What Is Critique?” and “The Culture of the Self”, the May 27, 1978 lecture and the “art of not being governed like this.”
  • Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Michel Foucault”, an overview of his work on surveillance and discipline.

item.title: When Watching Students Becomes the Lesson
item.description: Schools collect more data on students than ever. They should have to show it helps, explain it, and let people push back when it is wrong.
item.content:encoded:
What do students learn when a school-issued device records what they search and write?

Student surveillance is a blunt policy with a weak case for trust. Schools are collecting more data about students than ever. A school should show a tool helps, explain what it does, and let people challenge mistakes.

The everyday practice

At 11 p.m., a ninth grader types a dark joke on a school-issued laptop. By morning, monitoring software has flagged it and an administrator has a report. Down the hall, an attendance app records three late arrivals for another student and triggers an automatic penalty. Some districts have also installed entrance cameras that match faces against a watch list.

The tools arrive through software updates, safety grants and new dashboard features, which can make surveillance seem routine. The philosopher Michel Foucault argued that modern institutions shape people less through force than through observation, records and ranking. When people do not know when they are being watched, they may start policing themselves as if observation never stops. Students learn the lesson plan, along with the sense that someone is always watching and scoring them.

This is already happening at a large scale. Gaggle says it works with about 1,500 school districts and tracks the online activity of roughly 6 million students. A U.S. Senate investigation found that more than 7,000 schools or districts used GoGuardian's monitoring products in 2021.

In Vancouver, Washington, the district paid Gaggle $328,036 for three school years. The software scans what students search and write on school-issued devices around the clock, then sends anything that matches its patterns to human reviewers and, after that, to the school.

Schools should care about safety and attendance. Monitoring has expanded faster than basic questions about whether it works, whom it harms and who gets a say.

Who defines “risk,” and whose knowledge counts

Each tool defines a problem through choices: a keyword list marks danger signals, a behavior points system labels disruptive actions, and a vendor's model decides what counts as a “concerning” search.

Those choices are usually made far from the classroom, by companies and administrators. The people who have the most context are rarely asked: the teacher who knows a student was quoting a song, the parent who knows why a child is late, or the student who knows what a phrase means in their community.

When the Associated Press and the Seattle Times examined Vancouver's records, they found that from October 2023 to October 2024 nearly 2,200 students, about 10% of the district, had been the subject of an alert. The system flagged more than 1,000 documents for suicide and nearly 800 for threats of violence, and many were false alarms. At one arts high school, about 1 in 4 students had written something that triggered an alert.

One student was flagged for a short story with mildly violent imagery. A keyword list had decided what that creative writing meant, without a teacher making that call.

A record can speak louder than the people who know a student. Foucault's point was that this is a form of power, even when everyone involved means well.

Who benefits, and who bears the costs

Monitoring offers easy-to-show benefits: administrators receive reports for the board, vendors get contracts, and districts can feel they have acted on safety.

The less visible costs fall unevenly:

  • Students who rely on school devices. Someone with a personal laptop can search privately at home. A student whose only computer is school-issued may still be monitored there.
  • Students already watched more closely. In a 2022 national survey by the Center for Democracy and Technology, 48% of Black students and 55% of Hispanic students said they or someone they knew had gotten in trouble because of monitoring, compared with 41% of white students.
  • Students who need help. In the same survey, 29% of LGBTQ+ students said they or someone they knew had been outed by monitoring without consent. A teenager searching for information about depression, sexuality or a family crisis may stop if they know the search could be flagged.
  • Students who were never asked. In the Vancouver records, at least six students were potentially outed to school officials after writing about being gay, transgender or struggling with gender dysphoria. In Durham, North Carolina, an advocate said a self-harm alert led to a student being outed to an unsupportive family, and the school board voted to stop using Gaggle in 2023. One Vancouver student, after learning about the monitoring, stopped searching personal health questions: “I was too scared to be curious.”
  • Students whose secrets leak. Information collected to protect students can expose them. Through a single public records request, reporters received almost 3,500 sensitive, unredacted student documents from Vancouver's monitoring system, with no password or firewall in the way. Gaggle changed its system afterward. Every record kept is also a record that could be lost.
  • Everyone's trust. Students who feel scored all day may learn to perform for the system and avoid asking honest questions.

Among teachers at schools using monitoring software, 78% said students had been flagged for discipline and 44% said a student had been contacted by law enforcement because of an alert. A flag can outlast the moment and follow a student in a file long after the situation has passed.

What the evidence and affected voices say

In some places, the public debate has already led to action. In 2020 the Lockport school district in New York switched on a $1.4 million facial recognition system. Two parents, represented by the New York Civil Liberties Union, sued, and the state paused the technology.

In 2023 a state report found the risks in schools “may outweigh the benefits,” including higher false-positive rates for people of color and transgender people, and warned it “may only offer the appearance of safer schools.” That September, New York's Education Commissioner banned facial recognition in schools.

Online monitoring has not faced the same test. Independent research has not shown that this software measurably lowers student suicide or violence. A 2023 RAND study found only “scant evidence” either way and concluded that “no research to date has comprehensively examined how these programs affect youth suicide prevention.”

The Vancouver officials interviewed by reporters said they do not track whether the tool works, though they believe it has saved lives. RAND published its report on Dec. 5, 2023, and says more data are needed to show how accurately AI algorithms detect suicide risk and whether the tools improve student mental health. The report itself lays out that gap.

New York's ban raises a question most communities have not asked: does monitoring make students safer, and at what price? Districts should answer it publicly, along with these questions:

  1. Which monitoring tools are in use, what they collect, and how long the data is kept.
  2. How many flags or automatic penalties were issued last year, and how many led to a real intervention.
  3. How those flags and penalties break down by student group.
  4. Whether a student or family can see what was recorded about them, and how to correct it.

Numbers are incomplete. Students, parents and teachers can describe how a flag felt, what it changed and whether anyone explained it. Their accounts belong beside vendor marketing claims.

One reform: a student data bill of rights

I would start with a school-board policy written with students, families and teachers. It could set four commitments:

  • Transparency. Publish every monitoring tool in use, what it collects and why, in plain language, every year.
  • Collect less. No monitoring outside school hours on school devices without a specific, documented reason. No facial recognition.
  • A human in the loop. A flag alone cannot trigger an automatic penalty or referral. Someone who knows the student reviews it first.
  • See it, challenge it, let it expire. Students and families can view their records, correct mistakes and appeal decisions. Minor discipline and risk notes expire after a set period, so they do not follow a student forever.

Students who need support still deserve it. A counselor can help a struggling student without making every conversation a permanent entry. Support should come with clear rules about who can see what. The default should be the least sensitive record that still lets help happen.

FERPA gives parents, and students once they turn 18, the right to inspect education records within 45 days of asking, request changes to inaccurate or misleading records, and seek a hearing if a school refuses. Few families know this. The law predates laptops that can generate an 11 p.m. report; a local policy could make these rights easier to use and clarify that monitoring flags and risk notes count as records too.

How to know if it works. After one school year, the district could report publicly on:

  • The number of flags and automatic penalties, compared with the year before.
  • How many flags led to real help and how many resulted only in a record.
  • Whether gaps between student groups narrowed.
  • How many records were viewed, corrected or expired.
  • What students and families say in a short survey about trust and fairness.

What I still don't know

The strongest case for monitoring is that it can sometimes identify a student in real danger, such as someone searching for ways to hurt themselves, and get help to them in time. The alerts are not all noise: one Oklahoma district received close to 1,000 alerts in the 2023–24 school year, 281 of them about suicide, and among the screenshots reporters reviewed was a student asking, “Why does my boyfriend hit me?”

Some of those flags point to real children in real trouble, and I take that seriously. That is why this proposal keeps human review and support, while stopping short of banning monitoring altogether. If a district's own numbers showed that its flags regularly led to real help, with little harm and no unequal impact, I would rethink how far these limits should go.

I still want to know how often an alert leads to a response a student experiences as helpful, and how often it leaves only a record behind. What would change if students and families could see and challenge a flag before it shaped a school decision?

What students learn

Schools teach more than subjects. When students are watched and scored all day, they may learn that a record matters more than they do. Seeing, questioning and helping write the rules can teach them that institutions must answer to the people they serve.

If your school uses monitoring software, bring the four questions above to your next board meeting. I want to know whether the answers lead to changes students can actually see.

Check it yourself

  • Read RAND's 2023 report on student activity monitoring and the questions it leaves open.
  • Read New York State Education Department's determination on biometric identification in schools.
  • Read the U.S. Department of Education’s FERPA overview on access to education records and requests to correct them.

Where the facts come from

Sources

  • Center for Democracy and Technology, “Students and Teachers Warn That Schools’ Use of Monitoring Software Is Harming Students” (August 2022), the survey figures on discipline, law enforcement contact, outing, and differences by race.
  • Associated Press and The Seattle Times, “Schools use AI to monitor kids, hoping to prevent violence. Our investigation found security risks” (March 2025), the Gaggle and GoGuardian figures, the Vancouver alerts and records leak, the Durham and Oklahoma examples, student quotes, and the RAND finding.
  • RAND Corporation, “Artificial Intelligence–Based Student Activity Monitoring for Suicide Risk” (December 5, 2023), the report's own summary of evidence gaps and recommendations.
  • WSKG / Associated Press, “New York bans facial recognition in schools after report finds risks outweigh potential benefits” (September 2023), the Lockport system, the NYCLU lawsuit, and the state report's findings.
  • New York State Education Department, determination on biometric identifying technology in schools (September 27, 2023), the ban on facial recognition in schools.
  • U.S. Department of Education, Student Privacy Policy Office, FERPA overview, the federal law on access to and amendment of education records.
  • Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Michel Foucault”, an overview of Discipline and Punish: observation, normalizing judgment, the examination, and the Panopticon.

item.title: A school should be a harbor
item.description: Eight small, testable ways to make a school feel safe: private help, a calm start, a quiet room, meals without shame, and rules that listen.
item.content:encoded:
Schools should make belonging practical, and this list gets most priorities right. Small moments decide whether school feels safe or unsafe. Can students take snacks without being watched or sit somewhere without trouble?

Does the lunch line announce who owes money? Students may forget a policy. They remember whether they felt wanted.

I am training as a family therapist, so I think about schools like homes. Rules matter, and the feeling under those rules matters too. These eight ideas give schools practical changes they can try without a big budget.

None needs a new law. Students should not have to explain or prove why they need any of them.

In the national 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, 55.3% of high school students agreed or strongly agreed that they felt close to people at school, the survey's measure of school connectedness.

1. A school should be a harbor

A sorting machine ranks students as they arrive. A harbor receives them.

A calm welcome at the door is basic, not a luxury. Every student should know one adult by name and where to find them. A simple catch-up plan could help students after they miss class. Missing a day should not cost students their standing in school.

2. Help without a spotlight

Some students need school supplies, hygiene items, or a snack. Asking for them in front of other people can feel uncomfortable. Students may go without those basics because asking feels exposed.

A school could put these items somewhere students can take them independently. No asking, forms, or proof of need should be required. A shelf, a drawer, or a corner of the nurse's office could work.

Then ask students privately whether the setup feels private and dignified. Fix the problems students identify. Do not leave them there.

This is the change I would start with. It is small, caring, and easy to test.

3. A soft landing before the first bell

A school could offer students a few optional, ungraded minutes before the first bell. They could use that time to settle, read, or sit near an adult they trust.

There would be no forced check-in and no sharing circle. Adults should not ask how students are doing unless they bring it up. The aim is to let the day begin gently, without searching for what is wrong.

4. Quiet is part of belonging

Students could help design a calm, accessible space that anyone can use briefly. No one would need to explain why they are there.

Two clear boundaries keep this space honest. It should never become a punishment room or a stand-in for real help. Someone may need more than quiet, and the space cannot replace that help.

If the same student is there daily, a caring adult has information to act on. The space should remain available for everyone.

5. The rules should hear the people who live under them

A school could choose one everyday policy, such as phones, hallway passes, or late work. Students could help shape that policy before it takes effect.

Adults should explain up front what can change, what cannot, and why. Then they should show students how their input affected the final decision. If it did not affect the decision, adults should explain their reasons.

Students can handle a no. Being asked and then ignored is harder.

6. Teach peace as a skill

Listening, repairing conflict, and disagreeing without humiliating someone take practice. Nobody is born knowing how to do those things.

Students could have optional practice that is short and low stakes. That practice should never become discipline. The aim is for students to know what to do after a fight. This holds, whatever the discipline records say.

7. The lunch table is part of the social contract

Students should be able to eat without shame over a balance their family owes. That debt should not become part of the meal.

A school could make nourishing meals easy to get. End lunch debt shaming in every form. That includes stamps on hands and taking a tray away.

Students should also have a real say in what is served. When a school feeds students without conditions, it says something about their worth.

8. A library should feel like a second living room

A school could keep the library open beyond class hours. Students could find books, internet, quiet, and an adult who helps. That adult should not ask why they need help.

For some students, the library is the only calm, warm, free place with Wi-Fi all week. Running it with that in mind matters.

What these have in common

Each idea protects privacy and choice. Students should not have to explain themselves or join in. A school could treat each one as a small experiment in dignity and belonging.

Try it for a semester, then ask students privately how it felt. Keep what students say works. Drop what they say does not.

I do not know how to make a whole school feel like a harbor. I am not sure anyone does. I want to start with the shelf.

A fair concern is that schools may not have the staff time or budget to implement these ideas, and a quiet corner or shelf cannot resolve larger needs on its own. Any change should be tested with students, who can say whether it feels private and useful.

What I still don't know

Which change would students choose first? How can a school hear from students who are least likely to volunteer an opinion?

Where to start this week

A school could start with help without a spotlight. Pick one shelf, stock it, and tell students nobody will ask why. A month later, ask a few students privately about the shelf.

Ask whether getting what they needed felt easy and dignified. That answer tells you more about the school than any test score. Then use what students say to decide what to change next.

Check it yourself

  • CDC's 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Survey report, including its measure and limitations.
  • The original 2023 national YRBS questionnaire, including the school-connectedness question.
  • CDC's 2023 YRBS results and school-connection strategies.

item.title: A Most Agreeable War
item.description: An essay in the manner of an old drawing-room novel: on the pride of the men who start wars and the prejudice of the people asked to cheer them on.
item.content:encoded:
How does a war become agreeable to people who may never pay its cost? War's sales pitch deserves a hard look. When a country has a large army, people start naming the enemy it needs. Who made that choice, and when did the rest of us agree?

In a September 2, 2026 overview, Brown University's Costs of War Project estimated that 905,000 to 940,000 people had died from war violence in post-9/11 war zones as of 2023. The estimate includes U.S. soldiers, allied security forces, civilians, and militants. Read the project’s overview and its estimates.

A fair counterargument is that force may be needed to stop an attack or protect people facing imminent harm. Leaders may have to act with incomplete evidence, and refusing to act can also carry serious costs.

The country called an enemy often gets little say in its story. It is like a rich young gentleman appearing in a neighborhood where families seek husbands. One season, no one mentions him.

The next, people at dinner recite his faults, though they could not find his country on a map. He has not spoken, yet everyone agrees he is dangerous and must be stopped.

On pride

War often starts with proud leaders who demand courage from other people's sons. They fear looking weak, then call that fear a principle. Their income can keep consequences far away, if they arrive at all.

When a war he backed goes badly, he may call its cause noble and its execution regrettable. The choices then sound like somebody else's, though somebody else made them. He will explain himself on television for twenty years. The soldiers who carried out his noble cause will be invited to wait on hold.

On prejudice

The proud men need the rest of us to supply prejudice. A war needs people who quickly choose the good side with little evidence, and a public that finds questions tiresome and doubts suspicious. A dinner slogan can make us feel part of something large.

I'm learning to watch for the pleasure in quick judgment. Disliking a whole people can feel easier than learning one person's name. A government's press office can hand us a costume for someone else's party.

On the people who pay

In an old novel, a bad marriage can ruin one family; a bad war ruins families across a town. A young man comes home unable to sleep. A city becomes a photograph.

A mother on the other side was never part of the argument. Proud men and a prejudiced public rarely pay the bill. The cost falls on people farthest from the conversation, which may explain why it is so easy to have.

What I am asking

I'm not asking anyone to love every government on earth. Some deserve contempt, ours included. I'm asking for a pause before taking a side.

Who sells this war, what do they gain, and will they be near it? Could we hear one person from the country we have been told to hate, in their own words, before agreeing that their home should burn?

What I still don't know

What evidence would let the public assess claims before supporting force? How can we hear from people in another country without treating one person as a stand-in for millions? Which checks on executive power work when Congress and the public disagree?

Changing your mind after judging someone too quickly can give a story a happy ending. If more of us admit we judged too soon, that could help end a few more wars. I want to practice taking a second look before deciding who deserves my contempt.

Check it yourself

  • Brown University's Costs of War overview for estimates and scope.
  • Constitution Annotated, Article I, Section 8 for Congress's war powers.
  • Congressional Research Service, The War Powers Resolution: Concepts and Practice for the law and its applications.

Where this comes from

Inspiration

  • Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen, free at Project Gutenberg. This essay borrows its mood, not its words: a story about judging people too fast, and the pride that keeps us from admitting it.

item.title: What I'm Learning About Third Parties
item.description: Most Americans say they want a third major party and almost none vote for one. A sourced explainer on why third parties lose, what they win anyway, and the reforms already changing the rules.
item.content:encoded:
Why do so many people say they want a third party but vote for one of the two major parties? Most Americans say they want a third major party. Almost none vote for one.

My working answer is that third parties get boxed out by the rules. I started reading because I wanted to understand that gap. Here is what I found, with the sources at the bottom and the uncertain parts marked.

The more I read, the more the rules looked like the main issue. Third parties in the United States lose for structural reasons. Their ideas and voters face a system that favors two parties.

Those structures can be changed, and a few states have already changed them. Until they change, the most useful thing a third party can do is make the big two steal from it.

I care because people feel shut out. Gallup has found for years that more Americans call themselves independents than Democrats or Republicans. In its Governance poll conducted September 1 to 23, 2023, Gallup found that 63 percent said the two parties did such a poor job that a third major party was needed, the highest share since Gallup first asked in 2003.

That is a lot of people who feel unrepresented by the only two doors they are allowed to walk through. Feeling unrepresented is bad for a country and, in my experience, bad for the people in it. The Gallup article also says the answer may register frustration with the two-party system, so it cannot tell us whether those respondents would support a particular new party or candidate.

The wall, brick by brick

The evidence points to at least five obstacles facing third parties in America. Any one could block a new party.

  • Winner takes all. Almost every US election awards the seat to whoever gets the most votes in a single district. A party that wins 20 percent everywhere wins nothing anywhere. In 1992, Ross Perot took nearly 19 percent of the national vote, the best independent showing in eighty years, and received zero electoral votes. In the 1950s, French political scientist Maurice Duverger noticed that this kind of system almost always settles into two parties, because voters learn not to waste a ballot. People call this Duverger's law. The label sounds absolute. The pattern is a strong habit, and it holds.
  • Getting on the ballot. Democrats and Republicans are usually on the ballot automatically. Other candidates have to petition state by state, across fifty different sets of rules for signatures, deadlines, and fees. Ballotpedia tracks those requirements, which range from a few thousand signatures to well over a hundred thousand in the biggest states. A new party can spend most of its money and volunteers just earning the right to lose.
  • Sore-loser laws. In most states, losing a party primary means you cannot run as an independent in the general election. That shuts off the most obvious path for a popular figure who falls out with their party.
  • The debate stage. Starting in 2000, the Commission on Presidential Debates required 15 percent in national polls to qualify for the stage. Perot got in during 1992 and was kept out in 1996. Nobody outside the two parties has cleared that bar since. In 2024, the campaigns went around the commission and arranged debates directly with television networks. The terms were similar, so the door stayed shut.
  • Money and the spoiler fear. Federal matching funds for the general election go to parties that got at least 5 percent last time, which almost none do. Donors and voters also worry that a vote for a third candidate helps the major candidate they like least. Whether that fear is justified in any given race is a real question. Florida is one place to look.

About the spoiler argument

In 2000, Ralph Nader won around 97,000 votes in Florida. George W. Bush carried the state, and with it the presidency, by 537. Democrats have not forgiven him. I cannot know how Nader's voters would have behaved without him.

Studies of exit polls suggest a chunk would have stayed home, while the rest would have split unevenly toward Gore. That probably still flips Florida. The word "probably" is doing some work there.

The honest version is that spoiling is real and rarer than the fear of it. The fear does most of the damage on its own. It scares people out of voting for what they actually want.

What third parties have done anyway

The historian Richard Hofstadter wrote that third parties are like bees: once they have stung, they die. The sting is the point. The Populists of the 1890s demanded a graduated income tax and the direct election of senators. Both are now in the Constitution, and the Populists are gone.

Eugene Debs ran as a Socialist five times, reached 6 percent in 1912, and lived to see the big parties adopt pieces of his platform. Theodore Roosevelt's Progressives took 27 percent that same year and pushed both parties leftward for a generation. The Republican Party began as a third party in 1854, replaced the Whigs within six years, and is the only one ever to do that.

More recent wins have been smaller and more local. Jesse Ventura was governor of Minnesota on the Reform Party line. Angus King and Bill Walker were independent governors of Maine and Alaska.

In Nebraska in 2024, Dan Osborn, an independent mechanic, ran for Senate with no party and lost by about seven points in a state Trump won by twenty. He is running again this year, and this time the Democrats stood down to clear his path. Democrats did the same in Idaho and South Dakota.

The 2026 candidates page has all of it. This is a new pattern. I do not know yet whether it is a fluke or a strategy.

The structures that are already changing

Three reforms get most of the attention. Each one already exists somewhere in the country.

  • Ranked-choice voting. Voters rank candidates, starting with their first choice. If that candidate is eliminated, the vote moves to the second choice. The spoiler problem mostly disappears. Maine uses it for federal elections, and Alaska uses a top-four primary with a ranked general election. Voters in Alaska narrowly kept the system in a 2024 repeal vote. On the other side, more than ten states have banned it outright, mostly with the argument that it confuses voters and slows counting.
  • Fusion voting. A small party nominates the same candidate as a major party, and votes cast on both lines are added together. The candidate sees exactly how many votes the small party delivered and owes it something. New York and Connecticut have used it for a century, and Oregon allows it too. Look at this year's ballots: Jeff Merkley and Ned Lamont both appear on the Working Families line. Fusion voting was legal almost everywhere until the 1890s, when the major parties banned it. That suggests they thought it worked.
  • Proportional representation. Multi-member districts let a party with 20 percent of the vote win about 20 percent of the seats. This is how most democracies elect their legislatures. A 1967 federal law requires single-member House districts, so changing that rule would take an act of Congress. That makes this the least likely of the three. A bill to do it, the Fair Representation Act, has been introduced and has not moved.

Who could be affected, and what might I be missing

The strongest counterpoint I found is that the two big parties are already coalitions. The Democratic Party contains people who would be three parties in Europe, and so does the Republican Party. Primaries are where those factions fight.

A motivated faction can capture a whole party, as Donald Trump showed in 2016 and Bernie Sanders nearly showed twice. That view makes primary challenges look like the better tool for change. The energy, on that view, belongs inside the parties.

Countries with proportional systems offer another fair warning. More parties can mean coalitions that take months to form and fall apart in a year. Israel, Belgium, and the Netherlands have all had long stretches without a functioning government. Two parties make for a crude system, though it usually produces a winner by morning.

People bear the costs of badly designed reforms. Reformers do not. Confusing ballots fall hardest on first-time voters, older voters, and voters working in a second language. Any change should be judged by how it treats them.

What I still don't know

Would more parties change representation without making coalition-building so unstable that voters lose trust? Which reforms can make votes feel more meaningful while keeping ballots accessible to people with different levels of time, language access, and election experience?

One step I want to take

Before November 3, I want to find out whether my state allows fusion or ranked-choice voting. If there is a ballot measure or a bill on either one, I want to learn who is behind it and who is against it. You can check your state too.

Start small: look at the "also on the ballot" column for your state on the candidates page, choose one name you have never heard of, and spend ten minutes finding out what they want. Most of them will never win. I still want to know what they are asking for.

Third parties lose largely because the rules were written by the people they are running against.

A separate explainer gives a fair summary of what the two big parties themselves stand for, and tries hard not to take a side. This post is not voting advice. It is a record of my reading.

Check it yourself

Gallup's poll is linked above. The National Archives Electoral College results page lets you check official outcomes, candidates, and election notes that include third-party candidates. The FEC election results page explains that historical federal results are compiled from state and territorial election offices, and where to check current certified results.

I want to keep checking which rules my state uses and whose voices the changes would make easier to hear.

Where the facts come from

Sources

  • Gallup, party affiliation trend, for the share of Americans who call themselves independents, and Gallup, October 2023, for the 63 percent who said a third party is needed.
  • National Archives, Electoral College results by year, for the Perot, Roosevelt, Debs, and Populist figures. Popular vote shares are rounded.
  • Federal Election Commission, official election results, for the 2000 Florida numbers, and the FEC's explanation of public funding, for the 5 percent rule.
  • Ballotpedia, ballot access requirements; Ballotpedia, ranked-choice voting, including which states use it and which have banned it; and Ballotpedia, fusion voting.
  • Commission on Presidential Debates, for the 15 percent polling threshold.
  • Maurice Duverger, Political Parties (1951), for the two-party tendency of winner-take-all systems. The effect is well documented but has exceptions, Canada and India among them.
  • Richard Hofstadter, The Age of Reform (1955), for the line about bees.
  • The 2026 candidates page on this site, checked against Ballotpedia, Wikipedia, and 270toWin, for who is on the ballot this year and where Democrats stood aside for independents.
  • What is uncertain: how Nader's 2000 voters would have voted without him, which exit-poll studies estimate differently; the exact count of states that have banned ranked-choice voting, which has been changing yearly; and whether the 2026 Democratic stand-downs are a trend. I will correct this post at the top, with the date, if any of it turns out wrong.

item.title: A Rest From Happiness
item.description: Being happy is good. Being expected to be happy all the time is work, and work needs breaks. On giving yourself permission to just be okay.
item.content:encoded:
Forced happiness is a second job with terrible benefits. Joy is good. Being expected to perform it all day is a bad deal. I want to think about what clocking out looks like.

I support joy. The problem is the schedule. Over the last few decades, happiness seems to have become something people are expected to produce and display, even though it can also happen on a good day.

Think of the smile at work, the upbeat reply to a message I do not have energy to read, and the gratitude list at bedtime when I would rather sleep. Each one can seem small. Together, they can feel like a second job, and I do not get much back for the work.

The job nobody applied for

Arlie Hochschild, a sociologist, gave this a name in 1983: emotional labor. She was writing about flight attendants who were paid to look delighted for eight hours. That idea reaches beyond airplanes. Many of us now do a version of it for free, at work, in group chats, and with relatives who ask how we are while visibly bracing for the answer.

Researchers who study this make a distinction between feeling an emotion and performing one. Performing an emotion you do not feel is called surface acting. The evidence on it is fairly consistent: people who do more of it report more emotional exhaustion and burnout than people who do less.

That result tracks. An evening spent being fun for other people can leave someone feeling hollow when they get home. Pretending has a cost, and it may show up later, when nobody is watching.

A 2011 meta-analysis of 95 independent studies found that surface acting was associated with impaired well-being. That is a reason to take the pattern seriously, though association alone does not show what caused what.

Why chasing it backfires

One finding surprised me. A group of psychologists asked people how much they valued being happy, then measured how happy they actually were. People who valued happiness most reported less of it, and that effect was strongest when life was going fine. The researchers suggested that a high standard for your own mood can make ordinary days feel like small failures.

You were supposed to feel great. You feel okay. Now you feel okay and disappointed about it. That is a lousy mood tax.

The same lab followed people over time and found a similar pattern in reverse: those who let difficult feelings be there without judging themselves for having them had better mental health months later than people who fought every low mood as it arrived. Decades of work on emotional suppression, the habit of pushing feelings down so they do not show, also links that habit with worse mood and less closeness with the people around you.

The limits matter. Most are correlational, which means they show that the pressure to be happy and feeling worse travel together, while leaving open which one drives the other. They also come mostly from one corner of the world. I still see them pointing the same way, and that fits what I notice: people most frightened of a bad day are rarely the people having the fewest of them.

What a rest actually looks like

My proposal is small: take a break from performing in a few places and pay attention to what happens.

  • Let a day be a six out of ten. A day can be a regular Tuesday, without a crisis or a triumph. I could leave it at six without searching for reasons it should have been a nine.
  • Answer honestly, once. When someone you trust asks how you are, I could answer "tired, honestly" in place of "good!" They might say "me too," though I cannot know how they will respond.
  • Do not fix a feeling the moment it shows up. I could give a feeling some time before trying to fix it. I could imagine letting it sit on the sofa for an hour, without offering it tea, and notice what happens when I do not rush to change it.
  • Skip the gratitude list tonight. If it helps, I can keep it another time. If it has become one more thing I feel I am failing at, it may feel more like homework.
  • Tell one person you are off duty this week. I could say, "I am not up to being fun right now, but I would like to see you." I cannot know how they will respond, but I can be honest about how much company I want.

Where I might be wrong

Positive emotions can do useful work. Research has found that moments of genuine joy and interest can widen your attention and help you build friendships and skills you may lean on later. I am glad people have those experiences. What concerns me is the pressure to be on the hook for them.

There is also a distinction I do not want anyone to miss. A break from performing happiness is different from a mood that has gone flat and stayed flat. If you have felt low or empty most days for a couple of weeks, if sleep and appetite have changed, or if nothing you used to like does anything for you anymore, it is worth talking to someone about it.

The practical side of this site is there for exactly that: how to find care, how to pay for it, and what to say on the first call. The crisis strip at the top of this page is there for the worst nights.

Some people are simply cheerful. I have met them. This post is not aimed at them, and they are welcome to carry on.

A fair counterargument is that wanting happiness itself can be harmless. A later study separates that wish from judging whether you feel happy enough, so the concern here is self-monitoring, not joy.

What I still don't know

How much of this pressure comes from other people and institutions, and how much comes from the standards I set for myself? What does an honest answer sound like when the person asking may not have room to hear it?

One step

This week, I want to ease off the performance in one place where I have been doing it. One group chat, one colleague, or one evening is enough. I can notice what happens without turning it into a test of whether the world ends. I do not expect it to, and I want to see whether Friday feels any different from last Friday.

Check it yourself

  • Hülsheger and Schewe's 2011 meta-analysis of emotional labor.
  • Zerwas and colleagues on aspiring to happiness versus concern about happiness.

Where the facts come from

Sources

  • Arlie Russell Hochschild, The Managed Heart: Commercialization of Human Feeling (University of California Press, 1983). Coined "emotional labor" and the distinction between surface acting and deep acting.
  • Hülsheger & Schewe (2011), Journal of Occupational Health Psychology. A meta-analysis of emotional labor studies: surface acting is linked with emotional exhaustion and burnout.
  • Mauss, Tamir, Anderson & Savino (2011), Emotion. "Can seeking happiness make people unhappy?" People who valued happiness more reported lower well-being, most clearly when life stress was low. Mostly correlational, with one small experiment.
  • Ford, Lam, John & Mauss (2018), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Accepting negative emotions and thoughts, rather than judging them, predicted better psychological health over time.
  • Gross & John (2003), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Habitual emotional suppression is associated with worse mood and less social closeness.
  • Fredrickson (2001), American Psychologist. The counterpoint: the broaden-and-build theory of why positive emotions matter.

item.title: How great thinkers are made
item.description: Six habits that build a sharper mind, from reading the originals to arguing with people who disagree.
item.content:encoded:
How do people become thinkers whose work lasts?

Great thinkers are built through sustained work on problems that matter. Aristotle, Hobbes, Madison, Arendt and Rawls became remembered names because they focused on real problems. They kept working on those problems.

Their reputations followed the work. That is less mysterious than the usual genius story, and more useful.

On November 22, 1787, James Madison's Federalist No. 10 opened by naming “the violence of faction” as a problem his argument would address. Read the primary-source text.

A fair objection is that this story can make lasting recognition sound like a fair reward for effort. Access to education, money, mentors, and publication has shaped who could sustain inquiry and whose ideas entered the record.

The goal is simple. Choose a problem that matters to you. Think about it carefully over time.

Here are six habits worth trying. None requires a dramatic origin story.

1. Read the originals, not summaries

A summary hands you a thinker's conclusion. The original shows how the thinker got there. I think that reasoning is where much of the learning happens.

Start with this shelf in political thought:

  • Plato, Republic
  • Aristotle, Politics
  • Machiavelli, The Prince
  • Hobbes, Leviathan
  • Locke, Second Treatise of Government
  • Hamilton, Madison and Jay, The Federalist Papers
  • Tocqueville, Democracy in America
  • Mill, On Liberty
  • Marx and Engels, The Communist Manifesto
  • Arendt, The Human Condition
  • Rawls, A Theory of Justice

Read slowly. Write questions in the margins. Ask each author what they feared. Political theories often respond to fears about society and government.

2. Write every day

An idea can seem clear until you try to explain it. Writing exposes the parts you have not figured out yet.

Write one short piece each day. State your position and give your reasons. A steady writing habit matters more than polishing each sentence.

3. Make the best case for the other side

Explaining an opposing view in terms its supporters recognize takes care. If you cannot make its strongest case, you do not understand it well enough yet.

Before making your own argument, write a thoughtful defense of the position you are questioning.

4. Test ideas against real people

Ideas drift from the people they describe when kept far from daily life. Politics concerns people. Pay attention to how they fear, bond, fight and change.

I am training as a family therapist. This is the habit I care about most. Time with real families can teach me about power, trust and belonging. Books alone cannot teach me those things.

5. Find people who will push back

Talking through an idea can expose gaps in your reasoning. A reading group, mentor or friend who disagrees can offer perspective alongside books.

6. Give it decades

Most books on this shelf came after twenty years or more of this work. Ideas take time to develop. Questions keep opening up as you examine them.

What I still don't know

Which problems stay worth attention once the first excitement wears off? How can I tell whether I am testing an idea or only gathering reasons to defend it?

After a week of reading and writing, I want to see which question still feels worth carrying into the next week.

Where to start this week

Choose one book from the list and read ten pages a day. Write a paragraph about it, then another responding to it. Repeat the practice and notice which questions keep coming up.

Check it yourself

  • Read Madison's Federalist No. 10.
  • Read Plato's Republic through Project Gutenberg.
  • Read Hobbes's Leviathan through Project Gutenberg.
